He worked tirelessly to strengthen its role whenever efforts were made to diminish it. he devoted himself to keeping the voice of multilateral action strong whenever attempts were made to silence it. Today, we meet at a crossroads. In many parts of the world, tensions are rising, conflicts are expanding, and crises are deepening. Meanwhile, trust among nations is declining. Isolationism and polarization are intensifying, whereas selfishness and exclusion are prevailing at the expense of cooperation. Unilateral coercive measures are increasingly being imposed, and the logic of power is once again reasserting itself, eclipsing the virtues of dialogue and disregarding the benefits of consensus and understanding. What sort of international order can function properly when principles are selected according to the identity of those who violate them? What confidence can remain in international law when the aggressor is granted the right to self-defense, while the victim is required to justify even the right to survive? And what future awaits humanity if imposing fait accompli and once again becomes a tool for managing conflict or determining their outcome. This matter is not simply a temporary crisis facing the international system, rather, it is a profound review of our collective conscience. and our capacity to preserve and develop the order we established after two world wars, so that future generations would not suffer the scourge of war. Because we failed to learn the lessons of a not so distant history, and because we did not heed these lessons and we did not transform them into measures that would protect us from the catastrophes of the past, finally and in full. And because we built a system of international relations whose central purpose was to reject war and to safeguard a lasting peace, but without providing this system with the means and instruments necessary to achieve an ambition of this size, For this reason, the theme that was chosen by the President of our General Assembly for this session, namely, Restoring Trust and Managing Transformation, a United Nations delivering results for all. This theme not only reflects the challenges of our time, but also prevents us with a fundamental question. How do we restore confidence in an international system whose rules and institutions have lost credibility? Algeria believes that the starting point must be from the place where the will of the international community must be embodied, namely the United Nations itself. this very place and this very hall particularly. It has become a necessity imposed by the profound transformations the world has undergone. It is imposed by the need for a more just international order, an international order that is more representative and more equitable. We cannot ask peoples to trust in multilateralism if its institutions continue to reflect the balances of a bygone era. We stress that correcting the historical injustice suffered by Africa requires permanent and fair African representation in the Security Council with full powers. If restoring trust begins with institutional reform, then it cannot be complete without doing justice to the peoples aspiring to self-determination and the realization of their national projects. My country follows with deep concern the continuing escalation in the Gulf region, where we are witnessing a conflict that is weighing heavily on the states and peoples of the region and is undermining their security and stability and threatening the welfare and development of their peoples, peoples that have found themselves held hostage to calculations that are not their own. and interests that are not their own. Algeria renews its condemnation of the violations of the sovereignty of states and their territorial integrity in the region. We stress the need to de-escalate and respect international law in addressing tensions, disagreements, and disputes that have Taken by storm, the region's digital ultimate aspirations for security, peace, and tranquility. The international community, and we along with it, welcomed the ceasefire in Gaza. that entered into force almost 11 months ago. We had hoped that it would mark the beginning of a process to end the suffering of civilians, that it would pave the way towards a lasting political solution. This is undoubtedly the correct and proper approach to addressing the situation of the last colony on the African continent. The passage of half a century cannot transform an imposed reality into a legal fact, nor can the passage of half a century transform an imposed reality and a right into a legal fact. or diminish a right whose holders need no one to explain it to them. The collective memory of peoples, such as is the historic experience of the United Nations, both confirm that genuine peace is not built by disregarding rights. Algeria views the Sahrawi Sahel region as a single space where the challenges of security, development, and stability intersect. As the President of the Republic, His Excellency Abdelmajid Taboun has stated, "Terrorism cannot be approached through a purely security-based method. nor can poverty and marginalization be effectively tackled in isolation from a security environment that enables terrorist groups and organized crime networks to expand and spread and take root. We will extend a hand and support political solutions that preserve the stability of the region and open before its people's broader horizons for development and progress. This leads us to a truth that cannot be ignored. Peace cannot be built without development, and development cannot flourish without security and stability. And under the leadership of the President of the Republic, Abdelmadjid Tebboune, Algeria has chosen to be an active participant in the changes that the world is witnessing today, not simply a recipient of these changes. Algeria has chosen to transform challenges into bridges towards progress, to transform its resources into levers for building a productive and diversified economy, and to use knowledge and science as engines of its comprehensive national advancement. Algeria has incorporated sustainable development into its national programs and enshrined it in the constitution since 2020. This is based on a vision that is grounded in social justice and in economic and environmental sustainability. The destiny of the peoples of the continent is interconnected. Their challenges are shared. This makes solidarity and integration in Africa, indispensable pillars of sustainable development. As we witness the accelerating technological revolution, we cannot accept that Africa would remain on the margins or simply become a consumer of its outputs. Here we note the need to invest in the African person to build scientific and digital capacities so that artificial intelligence becomes a tool for development, not a new label for another development gap between the North and the South. We call for a balanced and responsible international regulation of artificial intelligence that would guarantee equitable access to its benefits, that would preserve the sovereignty of states, and that would transform this revolution into a shared opportunity rather than an exclusive privilege or monopoly in the hands of a few. In the end, we return to the question where we began. How do we restore trust? Trust is restored when words match actions. Trust is restored when the law is applied equally to all. Trust is restored when peoples can see the United Nations as a common home, a shared home, rather than an organization held hostage to the dominance of power politics. Our responsibility today is not to leave to our children a legacy of a world that is burdened with our crises. Rather, what we owe them is to leave them a world that is better than the one that we have inherited. Let us move together forward, not because the path is an easy one, but because the alternative to cooperation is for each of us to face the storms of this era alone, isolated, and powerless. Let us make the restoration of trust a process rather than a slogan. Let us make multilateralism a reality rather than simply a principle. Let us make the United Nations in this pivotal moment A space where diplomacy regains its place, where confidence in institutions is restored, and where respect for international law becomes a shared commitment rather than a matter of convenience subject to whims. Let us work together for a world where the application of law is not a privilege, in which peace is not merely the temporary absence of war, and in which development is not reserved for those who came first, but rather a shared right of all peoples with all their diversity and for all generations to come. Mr. President, your excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor and privilege to deliver this statement on behalf of His Excellency, Professor Arthur Peter Mtharika, President of the Republic of Malawi, and the people of Malawi. I congratulate you, Mr. President, and all Vice-Presidents on your election to lead this one session of the United Nations General Assembly. Malawi pledges its full support to your leadership. We also extend our profound appreciation to the Secretary General for his unwavering dedication to our shared global values. Mr. President, the theme for this session, restoring trust, managing transformation, a United Nation that delivers for all. strikes at the heart of our current global reality. We live in an era of deep fractures. Trust between nations has eroded. Global systems are failing to manage rapid technological, economic, and environmental shifts equitably. For the United Nations to remain relevant, It must transform into an institution that delivers tangible progress for the most vulnerable, leaving no nation behind. I would therefore like to highlight six opportunities for restoring trust, managing transformation, and thereby ensuring a United Nations that delivers for all. The first opportunity is accelerating sustainable development and economic transformation. Mr. President, the timeline for the 2030 agenda for sustainable development is rapidly drawing to a close. Yet, the promise of the sustainable development goals remain dangerously out of reach for millions. For Malawi, the pursuit of wealth creation, self-reliance, and economic transformation is not merely a political aspiration. It is an urgent survival strategy. Because of this, we have remained steadfast in implementing the SDGs in alignment with our long-term development vision, the Malawi 2063. On this note, Mr. President, I'm happy to report that Malawi successfully presented our third voluntary national review during the 2026 ECOSOC high-level political forum, thereby reaffirming our commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Malawi 2063, as well as our desire to accelerate sustainable development and economic transformation. The review revealed that even though we face numerous structural challenges, we have made some progress on many of the SDGs. Mr. President, our goal is to systematically transform our economy by modernizing agriculture, expanding mining, and accelerating digitalization. However, National efforts alone cannot dismantle the structural barriers built into the global economic architecture. Developing nations require deliberate, scaled investment in industrialization, sustainable infrastructure, and regional value chains to transition from primary commodity exporters to diversified, industrialized economies. In addition, we cannot achieve sustainable development while drowning in debt. Malawi, therefore, calls for immediate comprehensive debt relief and restructuring. The current international financial architecture forces developing nations to choose between servicing predatory debts and investing in health, education, and climate resilience. This is a moral failure. Mr. President, we also call for a massive scaling up of concessional development financing. We need targeted investment in our key productive sectors, namely agriculture, industrialization, and infrastructure development as follows. agriculture modernization through mechanization and commercialization to guarantee food security. Second, building local industry so that we stop exporting raw materials and create decent jobs for our youth who make up nearly 40% of the Malawi population. And thirdly, developing robust transport, energy and digital infrastructure to connect Malawi to regional and global market. We therefore call upon our international partners to align their support with the national blueprint like the Malawi 2063 in order to generate meaningful job creation and shared prosperity. The second opportunity is strengthening climate action resilience. Mr. President, Malawi contributes negligibly to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet we remain on the front line of the climate crisis. In recent years, devastating cyclones, prolonged droughts, and increasingly erratic weather patterns have destroyed infrastructure, devastated crops, displaced thousands of our citizens, and inflicted severe damage on our economy. This year, we faced the added threat of El Nino-related extreme weather, which reached further undermining livelihood, food security, and economic stability. As such, we are fighting back by embedding climate resilience into our national development planning and strengthening locally-driven adaptation measures. However, our efforts are continually outpaced by the scale and speed of climate change. Climate shocks repeatedly destroy infrastructure, decimate agricultural production, and make worse food insecurity and erode hard-won development gains. Mr. President, the global community must therefore move beyond rhetoric and translate commitments into meaningful action. We call for the full and effective operationalization and capitalization of the loss and damage fund. Major historical and current emitters must honor their climate finance commitments by providing accessible, predictable, grant-based and highly concessionable financing, rather than relying on debt-creating instruments that further burden vulnerable countries already struggling to cope with the consequences of a crisis they did little to cause. Mr. President, Malawi therefore calls for enhanced, predictable and easily accessible climate finance with greater emphasis on adaptation and disaster risk reduction. We need sustainable investment in the early warning systems. Climate resilience infrastructure. Sustainable land management. Climate smart agriculture and locally led adaptation. Climate changes and existential threat to Malawi's development and to the hard won gains we have made. Mister President, The third opportunity is to reform global governance and strengthen multilateralism. The current global challenges underscore a fundamental truth. Our multilateral framework is fractured because its foundational architecture is obsolete. The institution designed in 1945 no longer reflects the geopolitical and economic realities of 2026. Malawi reaffirms its unwavering commitment to multilateralism, but it must be a multilateralism that is inclusive, fair and democratic. We call for an urgent, comprehensive reform of the United Nations Security Council to correct the historical injustice done to Africa. Africa deserves Permanent representation with full veto privileges are articulated in the Eswatini consensus. Furthermore, the international financing architecture, specifically the IMF and the World Bank, must be radically overhauled. The current system traps developing nations in cycles of unsustainable debt, forcing governments to choose between servicing foreign loans of funding basic education and health care for their citizens. Mr. President, because Malawi strongly believe in multilateralism, we take responsibility when called upon by the international community to participate in causes that further the aims of this organization. Malawi remains firmly committed to the rule of law, accountability, and the peaceful resolution of disputes. as indispensable foundation of an effective multilateral system. It is in this spirit that Malawi has presented the candidature of Lady Justice Thulane Chizumira for election as a judge of the International Criminal Court for the term 2027 to 2036. Justice Chizumira is a distinguished jurist with extensive judicial legal experience at the national, regional, and international levels, including her service as a judge of the African Court on Human and People's Rights. Her candidature reflects Malawi's commitment to strengthening international justice through experienced, independent, and highly qualified judicial leadership. As States Parties prepare to elect six judges to the International Criminal Court in December 2026, Malawi respectfully seeks the valued support of States Parties for the candidature of Lady Justice Yudirane Chizumira. We are confident that her extensive judicial experience, commitment to the rule of law, and demonstrated service to justice and human rights would enable her to make a meaningful contribution to the work of the court. Malawi looks forward to the support of fellow states, parties for her election, and to continuing our collective efforts to strengthen the institutions of international justice. Mr. President, the fourth opportunity for restoring trust Managing transformation and thereby ensuring a United Nation that delivers for all lies in strengthening global health security. Economic transformation and sustainable development are impossible without a health population. The vulnerabilities exposed by recent global pandemics continue to linger, reminding us that global health security is only as strong as its weakest link. Malawi is making strides towards achieving universal health coverage and strengthening our primary healthcare system. However, systemic global inequities in healthcare access, medical manufacturing, and vaccine distribution remain glaringly unresolved. True global health security demands decentralized pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities, unrestricted technology transfer and intellectual property waivers during health emergencies. My delegation appeals to all of us here to finalize a robust, legally binding pandemic treaty that guarantees equity, solidarity, and immediate resource sharing for the Global South. We also call for collaboration in efforts to build long-term resilience against pandemics through investment in our domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity. By producing essential medicine within Africa, the entire world gained through stronger health security and stable supply chains, especially through faster outbreak response. Mr. President, the fifth opportunity is to promote human rights, peace, and international security. Malawi firmly believes that development, peace and human rights are inextricably linked. We remain deeply committed to upholding the constitutional rights of all our citizens, strengthening our democratic institutions and maintaining an uncompromising stance against corruption. Furthermore, we strongly defend the right to development as an inalienable human right. True freedom cannot exist in condition of extreme poverty and systemic economic exclusion. On the global stage, we view with great alarm the proliferation of violent conflicts and constitutional changes of government, geopolitical fragmentation, and acts of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. Mr. President, the Malawi nation is not standing alone. As all these alarming developments occur, Malawi continues to play its part in global peace operations, deploying our brave men and women to United Nations peacekeeping missions to safeguard stability on our continent. In this regard, let me reiterate the call for immediate cessation of hostilities in all active conflict zones worldwide. Global resources currently being funneled into destructive warfare should instead be redirected towards eradicating poverty, building schools and financing sustainable development. We also reaffirm our solidarity with global efforts to combat racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. Mr. President, as we take steps to grab these opportunities, we must also recognize the emergence of artificial intelligence, which presents both opportunities and threats to humanity. Malawi welcomes the transformative potential for AI as an expression of human ingenuity and as an increasingly important tool for accelerating sustainable development. For developing countries, including Malawi, AI offers opportunities to strengthen agricultural productivity and food security, improve healthcare and education, enhance climate resilience and disaster preparedness, expand financial inclusion, and improve the efficiency of public service. Malawi believes, however, that technological advancements must remain human-centered. Artificial intelligence should complement and enhance human capabilities rather than diminish the indispensable role of people in shaping their own development. At the same time, Malawi recognizes that the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence presents significant challenges, particularly for developing economies with fragile labor markets and limited technological infrastructure. Automation could disrupt employment and widen existing inequalities, while unequal access to computing capacity, data, digital infrastructure, skills, and financing risks creating a new technological divide between and within countries. Malawi, therefore, calls upon the United Nations to continue promoting an inclusive, ethical, and development-oriented global framework for AI governance. One that safeguards human dignity and employment, builds the technological capacities of developing countries, facilitates equitable access to AI technologies, and ensures that the benefits of innovation contribute directly to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. No country should be left behind in the emerging AI-driven global economy. Mr. President, In conclusion, restoring trust requires honesty, accountability, and action. Managing transformation requires courage, vision, and solidarity. The choices we make today will reverberate for generations to come. We can choose to retreat into isolationism and protectionism, or we can choose to summon the political courage required to build a fairer, more resilient, and inclusive world. Malawi stands ready to play a part. We are transforming our economy, reforming our institutions, and investing in our people. But we cannot do it alone in an unfair global environment. We stand ready to work hand in hand with all Member States to bridge the divide, restore trust in multilateralism, and give a sustainable, dignified future for all humanity. Let this First session of the General Assembly mark the turning point where the United Nations transitions from a forum of speeches to an engine of delivery. Let us build a United Nations that delivers wealth instead of poverty, resilience instead of vulnerability, and peace instead of conflict, a United Nation that truly delivers for all. Thank you very much for your attention.
I thank the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Malawi. I now give the floor to His Excellency Wijetha Herath, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Sri Lanka.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, allow me at the outset to congratulate you, Dr. Khalilur Rahman, on your election as President of the 81st session of the General Assembly. On behalf of the Government of Sri Lanka, I wish you every success and assure you of our fullest support in the discharge of your mandate. We also convey our deep appreciation to your predecessor, Madam Annalena Baerbock, for her able stewardship of the 18th session. Let me also take this opportunity to acknowledge the leadership of Secretary-General Antonio Guterres as he concludes his term. Mr. President, seminal changes are taking place across the world at a pace faster than many institutions are able to adapt or respond. People across the globe are demanding greater clarity, honesty, and action from their leaders and institutions. The theme of this year's general debate, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, A United Nations that delivers for all goes to the heart of this challenge. The erosion of trust is reflected in unresolved conflicts, humanitarian crises that outpace available resources, increasingly frequent climate disasters, widening inequalities, and technological advances that are moving faster than governance. Together, These developments have contributed to a growing perception that global institutions are distant from the people they are meant to resolve. Sri Lanka understands this reality deeply. My country has, on many occasions in the past, experienced the consequences of deficits in trust and breaches of the social contract. Two years ago, marking a watershed moment in our history, the people of Sri Lanka, representing all communities and walks of life, gave a resounding mandate to the government of President M. W. Wickremesinghe to address these challenges and institute meaningful change. Since then, our government has been working with determination to rebuild trust from the ground up. We are building trust through action, not rhetoric, through delivery, discipline, and the courage to confront wrongdoing. Sri Lanka, too, is therefore undergoing a historic transformation and rejuvenation. Despite conflicts in several parts of the world, including in West Asia, and climate calamities, including the cyclone that struck Sri Lanka, my country has restored macroeconomic stability following the economic crisis of 2022. Today, Sri Lanka has been reclassified by the World Bank as an upper-middle-income economy, and ratings agencies have recognized this positive trajectory. However, these developments do not fully reflect the vulnerabilities of countries exposed to debt and external shocks. While we work with our global partners to consolidate this hard-won stability, we remain conscious of the critical need to address the hardships faced by vulnerable communities. Cyclone Dittha was one of the worst natural disasters in Sri Lanka's recent history and devastated several parts of our country. The calamity resulted in the loss of hundreds of lives and affected more than 2 million people. Livelihoods were disrupted and critical infrastructure was destroyed. Having experienced this tragedy, We understand deeply the challenge posed by the Himalayan floods to the people of Nepal and China. We extend our deepest sympathies to the victims. These tragic events demonstrate the enormous human and economic cost of climate change. Sadly, its harshest consequences continue to be borne by countries that have contributed least to global emissions. The call for action on climate impact is not merely immediate. It is overdue. Climate justice must become an urgent reality. For our part, Sri Lanka is on track towards achieving 70% renewable energy by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050. Mr. President, For three decades, Sri Lanka suffered a protracted conflict that caused enormous loss and suffering to all our communities. Although the guns fell silent 17 years ago, the deep wounds of that conflict remain, and much remains to be done to heal them. We are determined to prevent a recurrence of such a tragedy and to pursue a path towards national unity and reconciliation. In this regard, our government is strengthening national institutions to address outstanding issues. Throughout these two years, we have remained firm in our rejection of racism and religious extremism in all its forms and manifestations. We will continue to work tirelessly to build a nation that is more secure, inclusive, and united, a nation made stronger by the full richness of its diversity. Mr. President, in addition to the consequences of natural calamity, Sri Lanka, like many other countries, is experiencing the severe impact of conflicts in West Asia and elsewhere. As an island nation situated at the crossroads of the Indian Ocean, and as a country with a large number of migrant workers in West Asia, these developments have direct security, economic and social implications for us. I am pleased to note that even during these challenging times, Sri Lanka has continued to uphold its commitments to international law and ensure sanctity of human life and human dignity. Mr. President, in March this year, amidst a highly volatile geopolitical landscape, Sri Lanka found a ship of a party to a conflict in distress close to our territorial waters with many sailors life in peril. We took the difficult path of navigating a wilderness of sensitivities and marshalling our limited nations resources to rescue and look after the wounded and sick. Hard as it was, we went on to rescue hundreds more. We saw human lives in danger and we acted, founding ourselves on international law and on humanity. while safeguarding our neutrality we placed Humanity above all else as president thean has reiterated we will never hesitate to protect Humanity if there are actions that must be taken to protect human lives we will not hesitate to take them under any circumstance this Mr. President is the Sri Lanka we wish to bring before the world, a small island nation with a big heart which believes that even in times of conflict and profound division, there remains space for humanity. And that is also what we wish to see reflected in the world. We need a world where our capacity to uphold humanity grows faster than our capacity to destroy it. That is the transformation we should see. It is for these reasons that we are pained by the developments in Gaza and the occupied Palestinian territories. Mr. President, The global security environment has deteriorated significantly in recent years. It is difficult to accept that. In a world with so much wealth and knowledge, vast resources continue to be spent on weapons while children face starvation and are deprived of medicine and education. Sri Lanka remains deeply concerned by the conflicts in West Asia and by the heavy cost being borne far beyond the region. International law, including international humanitarian law, must be adhered to and respected by all parties. We reaffirm our position that dialogue is the only viable way forward. Sri Lanka continues to support the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination. We are among the countries that first recognized Palestine as a distinct state in the 1980s. We stand in solidarity with the international community in calling for an independent and sovereign state of Palestine. existing side by side with Israel in peace within the pre-1967 borders. We welcome the resolution of the Security Council on a ceasefire in Gaza and urge all parties to uphold it. Humanitarian assistance must reach civilians without obstruction. The recovery and reconstruction of Gaza must be an urgent priority. Mr. President, Sri Lanka is proud of its longstanding contribution to United Nations peacekeeping in pursuit of global peace and security, having deployed more than 21,000 personnel on numerous missions since 1957. Our blue helmets, through their dedication and service over many years, have earned the trust of local communities and the commendation of UN field mission. Today, they continue to serve with distinction in some of the most challenging environments under the UN flag, protecting vulnerable civilians, deterring violence, and helping war-torn communities transition from conflict to stability. Sri Lanka has also long championed multilateral disarmament. from our early call for an Indian Ocean zone of peace to our leadership at the 1995 NPT Review and Extension Conference. At a time of rising geopolitical tensions and rhetoric of nuclear escalation, We remain firmly convinced that the only real guarantee against these weapons is their total and verifiable elimination. Mr. President, as we approach 2030, we must deliver on the Sustainable Development Goals, which remain our collective blueprint for sustainable development. Sri Lanka once again calls for reform of the international financial system and for fairer rules governing debt and development finance. We welcomed the civil commitment last year, including its call for urgent action to close the $4 trillion financing gap for sustainable development in developing countries. It is now time to translate those commitments into concrete action. We remain steadfast in recognizing poverty and inequality as factors requiring our urgent attention. Our national budget last year made historic allocations to the healthcare and education sectors. We take pride in our longstanding policy of free and universal healthcare and education, and remain committed to strengthening these important pillars of social justice. while actively implementing all SDGs without discrimination. We fully subscribe to and proactively engage with SDG 16, which underscores the importance of just and inclusive institutions that build and restore public trust and treat all people equally. Mr. President, Sri Lanka has long championed and contributed towards a fair and peaceful order at sea under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, a legal regime which we have helped shape. We also support the work of the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf. We remain committed to preserving the oceans as a shared space for peaceful and sustainable use and for international cooperation. Our nation's prosperity is closely linked to the Indian Ocean. As founding member of the agreement on marine biological diversity of areas beyond nation jurisdiction, the BBNJ agreement, we reaffirm our commitment to safeguarding the oceans as a common heritage of humankind for present and future generations. We look forward to the further operationalization of the agreement, complementing the processes of the International Seabed Authority. Mr. President, one of the key pillars of the decisive mandate given to us by the people of Sri Lanka was to build a transparent and ethical nation. In delivering on this mandate, We have placed good governance, anti-corruption and institutional transparency at the core of a comprehensive national integrity drive that is being vigorously pursued. We have seen all too clearly how corruption weakens democracy and destroys trust. We continue to enforce the law against corruption without fear or favour, irrespective of a person's background or social standing. Investigations and prosecutions continue to progress without political interference. Substantial progress has been made in strengthening the independence of institutions responsible for investigating and prosecuting bribery and corruption. My President, who addressed this Assembly last year, also highlighted how narcotics and related organized crime have become a menace for many countries, as well as our government's comprehensive efforts to address this menace. One year on, our United as a Nation Anti-Narcotics National Program has made significant progress, including through the arrest of key figures in the narcotics supply chain. Mr. President, we reiterate our call on the global community to promote meaningful technology transfers, ensure equitable access for developing nations, bridge the digital divide, and build safe, secure, and trustworthy systems that leave no one behind. Sri Lanka is in the process of building a digital future that includes everyone. We have developed national AI ethical guidelines in line with international frameworks. We must ensure that emerging technologies and artificial intelligence are developed and used responsibly and consistently with international law, including the well-established principles of international humanitarian law. Their development and use must contribute to international peace and security while advancing humanity's collective interests. The interest of humanity must always guide the development and use of these technologies. Mr. President, for Sri Lanka, the United Nations is an indispensable partner. The UN has stood with us in challenging times and supported our development. For many of us in the developing world, the United Nations is also an expression of a fundamental promise that every nation, large or small, has a voice, that every people has a right to dignity and development, and that in an interdependent world, no country should be left to confront global challenges alone. For more than eight decades, amidst its flaws and with much room for improvement, the United Nations has given practical meaning to that promise. However, genuine faith in multilateralism requires the courage to acknowledge where the system has fallen short, the humility to listen to those who feel unheard, and the determination to make our institutions more effective, more representative, and more responsive. In this regard, Sri Lanka supports the UN80 initiative as an opportunity to renew and strengthen the United Nations and advance meaningful reform. Mr. President, Managing transformation cannot mean managing change for some while asking others merely to adapt to its consequences. The transformation taking place in our world must be inclusive. It must narrow rather than deepen the divides between north and south, between those who shape new technologies and those who merely receive them. and between those who possess resilience and those who are most exposed to global shocks. My country comes to this Assembly not with the expectation that the United Nations can solve every problem, but with the conviction that there are problems which no country can solve alone. Our answer must therefore be a renewed faith in multilateralism and a United Nations that listens more closely, represents more fairly, and delivers for all. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Sri Lanka. I now give the floor to His Excellency, Constant Sars Munda, Minister for Foreign Affairs, La Francophonie, and Congolese Abroad of the Congo.

Excellency, President of the 81st session of the General Assembly, Mr. Secretary-General. Your Excellencies, heads of state and government, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. Allow me to, before delivering the message of His Excellency Denis Sassou Nguesso, President of the Republic of the Congo, please allow me to express my very deep gratitude for the honor he has bestowed upon me by entrusting me with this mission, and I carry it out with respect loyalty, and a sense of duty, fully aware of the significance of faithfully conveying the national message entrusted to me today. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of the Congo congratulates the election of His Excellency, Mr. Halilu Rahman, as President of the 81st session of the General Assembly. We also pay tribute to Her Excellency, Ms. Annalena Baerbock, for her contribution to our work. And we further express our profound gratitude to His Excellency, Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary General of the United Nations, for his advocacy on behalf of Africa, his constant commitment to the Congo Basin, and his support to the peace mediation and dialogue efforts undertaken by our country. And in this regard, the Republic of the Congo is following very closely the selection process for the next UN Secretary-General. We believe that Africa, a continent at the center of many UN challenges and global geopolitical issues, must remain at the heart of the future Secretary-General's agenda. The next Secretary-General must embrace a truly universal vision of the United Nations, one that leaves no continent at the margins and which fully takes into account Africa's place, responsibilities, and legitimate interests. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, for the Republic of the Congo, restoring trust and managing transformation of our international institutions is a collective imperative. The theme of this session, Restoring Trust and Managing Transformation, resonates as a call for clarity and courage in a world where trust is eroding, tensions are rising, and double standards and relationships of force threaten to replace both the spirit and the letter of the UN Charter. Humanity has never needed renewed, inclusive, and representative multilateralism more than it does today. A multilateralism that can reflect the realities of a multipolar world in which Africa occupies a rightful place. This renewal requires a deep reform of international institutions, foremost amongst them, the Security Council. Africa strengthened by its history, its demographic dynamism and geopolitical importance, can no longer remain on the sidelines of decisions that shape its destiny. It must become a full and legitimate actor. In accordance with the Ezulwini Consensus, Africa's demand for two permanent Security Council seats with veto power is not a request, but a right, a legitimate right grounded, which reflects the realities of the 21st century. The world has changed, and our institutions must evolve with it. This is an imperative. And Africa is not asking for a favor. It is claiming its rightful place. The Republic of the Congo, as a member of the Committee of Heads of States and Governments of the African Union on Security Council reform, the C-10 Committee, will not compromise on this shared demand. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of the Congo reiterates its willingness to serve the international community With your support, we renew our aspiration to serve as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council for the 2030-2031 term. This candidacy of ours is rooted in a long diplomatic tradition, our sustained commitment to peace, and a strong sense of international responsibility. For more than five decades, Our diplomacy has contributed constantly and effectively to numerous peace processes on our continent, and which also had global implications. And let me quote the following, our contribution to supporting Namibia's liberation and then the withdrawal of Cuban troops from Angola through the 1988 Brazzaville Protocol, the efforts to end hostilities in the Central African Republic, Initiatives to promote reconciliation in Libya, where my country leads the African Union High-Level Committee. Also, the peace efforts in the Great Lakes region. Our diplomacy is not a diplomacy of confrontation. It is diplomacy based on dialogue, mediation, mutual respect, and African solutions to African problems. We reaffirm here and now the Pan-African vocation of our diplomacy and our commitment to international law. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, sovereignty is not a rejection of cooperation. Sovereignty is the ability of a people and a nation to freely determine their priorities, to defend their legitimate interests, to choose their partners, and to preserve their independence in decision-making. This is the understanding of sovereignty that the Republic of the Congo upholds. And we intend to continue pursuing a foreign policy based on non-alignment, diversification of partnerships, mutual respect among states, and the rejection of any foreign interference in domestic affairs. We are open to the world, but we intend to remain masters of our choices and our destiny. The Republic of the Congo does not seek to choose one camp against another. Rather, we seek to be a bridge between nations. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of the Congo has embarked upon a profound transformation through our national roadmap, which is called Let's Accelerate the March Towards Development. And it includes the following priorities: investing in human capital. Promoting youth employment, strengthening public governance, diversifying the economy, modernizing agriculture and industry.

Expanding infrastructure, accelerating digital transformation and innovation, and consolidating peace and social cohesion. We are building a Congo that does more than export raw materials. We aim to process and add value to our resources domestically. This explains our interest in special economic zones, because we think political sovereignty must go hand in hand with economic sovereignty. Our vision, I would like to point out, aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals, the SDGs, and the 2063 African Union agenda, the Africa we want. But let's be lucid and pragmatic here. The ambitions of our development at the Republic of the Congo and many other African countries are impeded by the burden of debt, inequalities in the international financial system, and the consequences of climate change. Four years before the 2030 SDG deadline, we cannot afford another collective failure. The Republic of the Congo, therefore, calls for an ambitious international action on the issue of developing country debt, including through debt relief and, where appropriate, debt cancellation measures to free resources for SDG-related investments. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Africa is not the world's periphery. It is one of its centers of gravity and a source of multilateral renewal. When Africa speaks with one voice, it advances the international agenda and inspires the world and opens new perspectives. Three major initiatives by my country illustrate this. The United Nations Decade for Afforestation and Reforestation 2027 to 2036, which was promoted by my country, the Republic of the Congo, Resolution 80/250 the transatlantic slave trade, recognizing it as a crime against humanity, which was promoted by Ghana, and the correct the map resolution promoted by Togo. These initiatives show that Africa contributes towards defining the international agenda. It is in this spirit that the Republic of the Congo will continue with its commitment to Africa. The removal of the visas as of the 1st of January 2027 for Africans promotes free movement into African tourists and solidarity amongst African people, making our trade more inclusive, all the while promoting the African Continental Free Trade Area. Ladies and gentlemen, your excellencies, the duty of memory also forces us to look at our history squarely in the eye. We are working on a major historical memorial, the Elongo Bay Memorial. From this region, countless people were torn from their families and homeland through the transatlantic slave trade. Luango must become a place of truth, remembers, reflection, but also a place of renewal. Our ambition here is to make Luango like a Goree in Senegal, like Cape Coast in Ghana, or Ouidah in Benin, should become a bridge between Africa and its diaspora. The people of African descent worldwide can reconnect with a history, identity, and dignity there. This is also the rationale of our 2025 meetings in Harlem or with people of African descent. Your Excellency, ladies and gentlemen, we also reaffirm our determination to mobilize Congolese living abroad. Our diaspora is a human benefit, an intellectual one, scientific and economic one. Its competencies, its experience, its investments, commitment are needed to accelerate our own development. We need all of our children to realize our human capital. The Republic of the Congo is a land of opportunity. It's endowed with natural resources, with critical minerals, with agricultural potential, with tourism potential, which has not yet been developed, our expanding infrastructure, and a strategic location at the heart of Central Africa. And we invite investors and development partners to join us through, for example, mutually beneficial public-private partnerships. We want the partnerships that create added value, develop our national competencies, promote technology transfer, respect our interests. and help us manage and develop our economy. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of the Congo also bears a special responsibility for the Congo Basin, which is the world's second largest environmental lung. This exceptional ecosystem contains immense biodiversity and plays a crucial role in regulating the global climate. The Congo Basin is one of Africa's principal contributions to the fight against climate change. We cannot continuously accept that countries preserve these ecosystems on their own, bear the cost alone. Conservation has a cost, and international solidarity must also have a value. We therefore call for fair and predictable compensation for ecosystems and carbon services, for innovative sustainable financing mechanism, increased capitalization of the Blue Fund, and for the recognition of the Congo Basin as a global priority and with the strengthening of international cooperation aimed at preserving it. We support a United Nations institution in the Republic of the Congo dedicated to the preservation of the basin. We also are asking for launching of a decade of the United Nations on afforestation, reforestation, and national plans for the implementation. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, above and beyond our rivers and forests, the tourist of the territory of the country is more than a geographical space. It is the foundation of our nation. the basis of our identity, the territory for our sovereignty. The Republic of the Congo will always defend the integrity of its territory, the security of our borders, mastering our resources and the freedom of our strategic choices. Our sovereignty is not negotiable. It is the responsibility that we owe to future generations, the inheritance that we need to bestow on future generations. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. We are a defender of peace internationally, and we are therefore call for negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, for de-escalation in the Strait of Hormuz, a just and lasting political solution in the Middle East and in Palestine. We call for the stabilization of Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, return of the lasting peace in Sudan, continued reconciliation in Libya, lifting of the embargo against Cuba, restoring of peace and stability in the Sahel. We reaffirm that peace is not weakness. that negotiation is not surrender, that dialogue is not capitulation. And in this spirit, we will continue to prioritize mediation, dialogue, and looking for peaceful political solutions so as to build Africa, which is prosperous and in peace from Libya to Sahel, from Sudan to Great Lakes. We reiterate the fact that we are available to accompany our brotherly countries in their work to achieve return to peace and stability. Through our history, we know that peace is difficult to build, but it is the only victory that benefits one and all. Ladies and gentlemen, your excellencies. guided by the same sense of responsibility. The recurring Ebola outbreaks and repeated pandemics have shown that global threats are no longer solely military or economic. Health security has become an essential component of collective security. And here, we will continue supporting the strengthening of the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa in Brazzaville and will shoulder all of its responsibilities in accordance with the 1952 Headquarters Agreement. We also call for international governance of artificial intelligence in outer space. These technologies must remain in the service of humanity, progress, and the empowerment of peoples. Technological progress must not become a new instrument of domination. Africa must also be a center of creativity, innovation, and digital sovereignty. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, to conclude, the Republic of the Congo remains faithful to its principles, peace, development, sovereignty, good neighborliness, dialogue, cooperation, and mutual respect amongst nations. We will continue to defend our national interests while fulfilling our international responsibilities. We will continue to believe in Africa and in our shared destiny, and we will continue to choose the United Nations as a privileged space for dialogue amongst people. I thank you.

I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs, La Francophonie, and Congolese Abroad of the Congo. I now give the floor to His Excellency, Muhyiddin Salim Ahmed Ibrahim, Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Sudan.

In the name of Allah, the most merciful and gracious, peace and blessings be upon our prophet and his family and his companions. Your Excellency, Mr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the General Assembly at its 81st session. Your Excellency, Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, esteemed delegations. At the outset, I wish to congratulate Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the General Assembly at its 81st session. I wish him every success in the discharge of his duties. I also extend my appreciation and gratitude to Ms. Annalena Baerbock for her capable stewardship of the previous session. I would be remiss not to express our appreciation to His Excellency, Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, for his defense of legitimate causes and his protection of the Charter. He has exerted considerable efforts to advance the reform process and to put forward initiatives aimed at making the United Nations more effective, influential, and representative. I stand today before this distinguished Assembly under deeply regrettable circumstances that Sudan never wished to witness within an organization founded on the principles of sovereign equality among states, respect for international law, and the guarantee of equal participation for all member states. His Excellency, General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, Chairman of the Transitional Sovereign Council of the Republic of Sudan, was to stand before you today to address the General Assembly on behalf of the Sudanese people and government. However, the host country prevented this by failing to issue the visa required for His Excellency to participate in this high-level segment of the General Assembly. More regrettably still, this situation persisted despite the efforts undertaken by the Secretariat and despite the Secretary-General's request to the host country to issue the entry visa in accordance with its obligations. under the 1947 Headquarters Agreement. Parallel and measurable measures to protect civilians, reduce polarization, de-escalate tensions and contain political estrangement among civilian, political and military forces. The dialogue being conducted through a purely Sudanese will, free from external interference and free from bargaining, intimidation and coercion practiced by some parties at present. Mr. President. The state has already begun preparations and creating a conducive environment for this dialogue aimed at reaching common ground through free discussion and placing the country on the path towards the most appropriate and inclusive political transition that excludes no one except outlaws and traitors. This transition should ultimately lead to free and fair elections in which all Sudanese participate under international and regional observation, allowing our people to determine who governs them at the conclusion of the democratic transition. On this basis, We affirm our readiness to cooperate constructively with initiatives aimed at addressing the root causes of the crisis, ending the unjust aggression against our people, preserving national state institutions and sovereignty, supporting efforts to achieve peace and development, and overcoming current challenges. We will support you when you do. So we ask you to be active in seeking an end to the horrific conflict in Sudan. You must be bold in pressing for a sustainable and just end to Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine. one that is consistent with Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity and the core principles of the Charter. We ask that you use your influence to progress a fragile ceasefire into a sustainable, durable peace. and you must be resolute in preserving conditions for a two-state solution. You must take the initiative, despite the challenges and entrenched views, to achieve a just and lasting resolution, where Israel and Palestine can live side by side within secure and clearly defined borders. We urge you to use your good offices to secure a lasting end to hostilities in the Persian Gulf and restore freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, which is a right guaranteed under international law. Of course, you cannot do this alone. For our part, as member states, we must provide you with the tools, the resources, and above all, the political support to ensure you can play this role effectively. Parties to conflicts must engage with you constructively and in good faith, while global and regional partners with influence must provide the necessary incentive for the parties to do so. The UN Security Council needs to fulfil its responsibilities. Permanent members in particular must act in a manner consistent with their special responsibilities under the Charter. Too frequently has the veto or the threat of the veto been abused to block the Council from fulfilling its responsibilities, to the frustration and sometimes despair of the global community. Inevitably, the costs of this failure are borne by those caught in conflict. This Assembly also has a legitimate and necessary role to play in maintaining peace and security. and we have been pleased to see it step up on occasions when the Security Council has been stymied from acting. For our part, New Zealand will continue to press for a more effective, credible, transparent and representative Security Council. As a demonstration of our continued commitment to collective security and the UN Charter, New Zealand is seeking a seat on the UN Security Council for 2039-40. We ask the next Secretary-General to work with us to preserve the integrity of the global disarmament framework, particularly on weapons of mass destruction. The grave dangers of deterioration of the global non-proliferation regime should alarm us all. New Zealand was deeply disappointed at the failure to reach consensus at this year's Nuclear Non-Proliferation Review Conference. After three consecutive Review Conference failures, we must do all we can to preserve the health of the NPT and indeed strengthen it. This means tackling persistent violations and cases of non-compliance. Iran is not in compliance with its nuclear safeguards obligations. The DPRK's nuclear weapons and missile programs continue to threaten its region and beyond. Halting the NPT's deterioration also requires concrete action from nuclear weapon states, to, at long last, chart a path towards total, verifiable and irreversible nuclear disarmament. We also call on you to safeguard the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the constitution for the oceans, which provides the framework within which all activities in the oceans and seas must be carried out. Compliance with these universally applicable rules is essential, not only for maintaining peace and security, but also for protecting prosperity and food security, given the ocean's vital role in supporting trade. Second, we call on the next Secretary-General to provide strong leadership across the UN's development and human rights pillars. The authors of the UN Charter understood that peace and security cannot be sustained without creating the conditions for member states to provide their citizens with prosperity and the full enjoyment of human rights. With significant changes in the global development cooperation landscape, we ask you to ensure that the UN is clear about where its comparative advantage lies. alongside the role of governments, regional organizations, and international financial institutions. Citizens and donors expect the UN to operate as one, with agencies working together through a strengthened resident coordinator system. We will work with you to ensure the UN is more coordinated and focused on strengthening local capacity and partnerships to address a country's development needs. The UN development system must remain relevant, responsive and accessible to all member states based on need, rather than size, income level or location. We welcome progress in advancing the UN's multidimensional vulnerability index and want to see further work to ensure its practical application across the multilateral development system. In the face of contracting development finance flows and increasing debt levels, we need to ensure our ambitions are matched by more sustainable and predictable financing. This will inevitably involve moving beyond exclusive reliance on traditional sources and approaches. President, as Pacific Island Forum leaders recently reaffirmed in Palau, Climate change remains the single greatest threat to the livelihoods, security, and wellbeing of Pacific peoples. While New Zealand will play its part, our efforts will mean little in the absence of determined action by the world's major emitters. Rising sea levels continue to threaten the viability of many communities and pose a threat to low-lying island states. including some of our Pacific neighbors. The political declaration on sea level rise endorsed this week is a potent demonstration of the UN's ability to address contemporary challenges affecting its members. We particularly welcome the declaration's affirmation of the preservation of maritime zones and the presumption of continued statehood, notwithstanding sea level rise. We also expect the new Secretary-General to defend international humanitarian law and international human rights law and its institutions. The promotion and protection of universal and indivisible human rights is fundamental to the world we live in today and to a collective vision of our future. Societies in which citizens can enjoy their universal human rights have a better chance of avoiding the descent into conflict that tragically impacts so many across the world today. Over the past decade, these norms have often been under threat, sometimes through neglect, sometimes through deliberate and sustained attacks. The rise of attacks on protected individuals, including civilians and humanitarian and medical personnel, needs particular attention. It is now 10 years since New Zealand co-led the adoption of Security Council Resolution 2286 on healthcare in armed conflict. Attacks on medical facilities and personnel in violation of international humanitarian law have grown exponentially worse since then. Few have been held accountable for these flagrant violations of international humanitarian law. We ask you to help us reverse these trends. by drawing on the UN's unique legitimacy to call out egregious and systematic violations of these norms, wherever they may occur and whoever may be perpetrating them, and by providing practical guidance and assistance to help member states meet their obligations. Third, we ask the new Secretary-General to maintain momentum and ambition on UN reform. Confidence in this institution depends on its ability to deliver impact. The next Secretary-General must work with Member States to chart an ambitious vision for the next phase of reform, while ensuring implementation of the decisions already taken. At a time of multiple and overlapping crises and growing constraints, we need a United Nations that is focused on its core tasks disciplined and accountable. One where every dollar delivers maximum impact. One that measures success, not by the number of mandates it creates, or the meetings it holds, but by the difference it makes in people's lives. Meeting this challenge means exercising your powers to achieve the most impact from the resources available. It means demanding a culture of continuous improvement, one that focuses on effective implementation and results. It means setting the highest standards for performance within the secretariat and holding staff accountable for delivering. In this regard, we ask you to demonstrate independence in your senior appointments. New Zealand has never accepted the right of any country to assert ownership of UN positions by virtue of power or status. We encourage Secretary-General candidates to commit publicly to making senior appointments on the basis of merit. Reform is a joint responsibility. We as Member States must avoid the trap of regarding reform as something that others will deliver for us. and instead live up to our own responsibilities in building the organization we need. We cannot expect the UN to continue to lurch on in a state of constant financial crisis. Member states must meet their financial obligations in full, on time, and without conditions, in accordance with their obligations under the Charter. We need to focus our attention on the issues that really matter and that can genuinely deliver benefits for our citizens. Resolution 82/51 equips Member States to tackle the long-standing challenge of mandate accumulation and overload. It commits us all to take a more disciplined approach to setting the organization's priorities. It provides the framework we need to create a more focused, coherent, and impactful UN. Yet its success will depend on whether we are willing to act differently. If we aren't prepared to make the necessary choices, we will be left with an ever-growing set of responsibilities supported by an ever-shrinking pool of resources. That will do nothing to strengthen confidence in the UN's relevance and effectiveness. Reform begins with us. It requires member states to make the decisions that only member states can make. That is the only way we can truly achieve an organization that is fit to meet the challenges that lie before us and that our citizens need and expect. Fourth and finally, we urge the next Secretary-General to ensure that the UN works for all states. The sovereign equality of states is one of the most central principles of the UN Charter. It must be central also to your approach. The fundamental premise of the United Nations is that every state, regardless of size or circumstance, has a stake in shaping our shared future. We also call on the President of the General Assembly to remain a steadfast champion of the voices, prerogatives and interests of the entire UN membership across all pillars of its work. The next Secretary-General's leadership in these areas will be essential, but we must also find it in ourselves to demonstrate leadership. Ultimately, the health, relevance and effectiveness of the United Nations depends primarily on its members, not its Secretary-General. As Member States, we must acknowledge our role in the financial and legitimacy crisis facing the UN. We must ask whether we have the collective will to change our behaviour. Do we have the discipline to focus our attention and resources on the issues that really matter to our citizens and deliver impact to their lives? Do we have the honesty to admit what is working and what is not? Do we have the will to invest in the multilateral system, both politically and financially, to enable it to deliver results where we can truly make a difference? coupled with the courage to make bold and consequent decisions on UN reform that can deliver a more effective organization. Collective action has changed the course of global challenges before. These achievements were not inevitable. They were the result of political leadership, persistence, and a willingness to work together despite differences to build understanding and compromise. The most fundamental step we can all take to revive this organization is to unequivocally recommit ourselves, both in words and deeds, to the principles that the Charter requires us to follow in our relations with other states. Respect for sovereignty, international law, the pursuit of dialogue and cooperation, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. At a time when conflict is rising, trust is eroding, and geopolitical competition is intensifying, we should not conclude that multilateralism has failed. We should conclude that it is needed more than ever. Thank you.

Can international law restrain power rather than merely record its consequences? Can development remain a promise for all rather than a privilege for some? For Antigua and Barbuda, These are not philosophical questions. For small island developing states, these are questions of survival. As we begin the 81st session of this General Assembly, we stand between two eras, one ending and another waiting to be shaped.
