And even as we respond to the security crisis, humanitarian assistance must remain at the center of our efforts. Mr. President. Grenada remains deeply concerned about the continuing hardship endured by the Cuban people. Our humanitarian conscience cannot be indifferent to the circumstances of ordinary households, particularly children, the elderly, and other vulnerable persons, whose difficulty deepen with each passing day that the present impasse remains unresolved. We call for constructive engagement that places the well-being of the Cuban people at its center and opens a path toward meaningful relief, improved living conditions, and renewed opportunities. This requires Cuba and the United States of America to address the very difficult but not insurmountable challenges of ending of sanctions, the removal of the embargo and blockade against the Cuban people. And importantly, the necessary reforms required to ensure the continued well-being of the Cuban people. Some of such reforms, Grenada notes are already being undertaken. Mr. President, as we speak of transforming our multilateral system, we must also ensure that its leadership reflects the diversity, experience, and aspirations of the people it serves. Grenada therefore proudly joins the CARICOM family in giving or unequivocal support to the candidacy of Ambassador Carolyn Rodriguez Bickett of Guyana for the position of Secretary General of the United Nations. CARICOM heads of government have endorsed her as the region's candidate. recognizing the experience and leadership she brings to this important moment for global multilateralism. Her distinguished service as Guyana's foreign minister and permanent representative to the United Nations has demonstrated a deep commitment to diplomacy, dialogue, and international cooperation. The Caribbean has long demonstrated that size does not determine the strength of our ideas, the quality of our leadership, or the values of our contribution to the international community. We believe Ambassador Rodriguez Bocket is eminently qualified to serve the entire United Nations membership. Her election would represent a historic milestone for Caribbean region and a powerful affirmation that every region including small island developing states can contribute to leadership at the highest level of a multilateral system. Mister President, We meet at a time of significant global transformation. The challenges before us are complex, but they also present an opportunity to renew our commitment to cooperation and create practical solutions that improve the lives of our people. The theme of this session, Restoring Trust, Managing transformation, a United Nations that delivers for all, challenges us to move beyond declaration towards delivery. For Grenada, removing trust means demonstrating through our actions that international cooperation produces results. It means listening to one another. It means respecting the voices of small states as much as those of large ones. It means building genuine partnership. And it means ensuring that every country has the opportunity to pursue its legitimate development aspirations. Grenada approaches this general assembly in a spirit of partnership, optimism, and constructive engagement. We remain firmly committed to the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations, international law, peaceful dialogue, and the peaceful settlement of dispute. In an increasingly interconnected world, cooperation is not merely desirable, it is indispensable. Mr. President, The transformation we advocate internationally must also take place at home. Grenada is advancing an ambitious long-term road map towards our 75th anniversary of independence. Anchored in our national sustainable development plan of 2020 to 2035, vision 75 charts a transformational course for our nation. Rooted in sustainability, resilience, equity, and opportunity. At the heart of Vision 75 are five strategic pillars: education and skill training, healthcare, agriculture and food security, the environment and energy, and housing. These are not simply sectors of government policy. They are investment in people. We are investing in health and wellness, education and skills, food security, renewable energy, digital innovation, and environmental sustainability. We are creating greater opportunities for young people and preparing them not simply for the jobs that exist today, but for the industry they will define tomorrow. For Grenada, transformation must always be people-centered. It means building resilience while creating opportunities, expanding our economy while protecting our environment, and embracing technology while safeguarding humanity. Mr. President, as a small island developing state, Grenada understands resilience. But experience has also taught us that resilience cannot begin after disaster strikes. We must invest before the storm, prepare before the emergency bill, before the damage is done, and finance resilience before countries are forced to borrow simply to rebuild what they have lost. This requires Greater international cooperation in climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, resilient infrastructure, and accessible financing. Small island developing states should not be viewed simply as victims of climate change. We are also laboratories of resilience. Climate action remains one of the areas in which collective effort can make a profound difference. Grenada remains committed to strengthening resilience and advancing sustainable and low carbon development. But ambition without implementation is merely aspiration. For vulnerable countries, climate commitments must be accompanied by reliable access to the resources required to deliver them. Climate financing must become more accessible, predictable, and responsive. Our objective should not simply be to help vulnerable countries recover from the next disaster. Our objective must be to transform vulnerability into resilience and resilience into sustainable opportunity. Mr. President, this transformation must also take place in the international financial system. Grenada welcomes growing recognition that development and vulnerability cannot be accessed by income alone. The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index offers an important opportunity to better recognize the structural circumstances of small island developing states. Our vulnerabilities are shaped by exposure to climate change, natural disasters, external economic shocks, and other circumstances that cannot adequately be captured through income per capita. Grenada, therefore, encourages Member States, development partners and international financial institutions to advance vulnerability-informed approaches to development financing. Greater access to concessional financing, climate finance, disaster risk financing, and innovative financial instruments can help countries move from vulnerability to resilience and from recovery to sustainable growth. Mr. President, at the center of all of this must be our young people. Their creativity, energy, and ideas are among our greatest national and global assets. Our responsibility is to give them the education, skills, technology, and opportunities necessary to shape the world they will inherit. Digital transformation and emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, offer enormous possibilities for education, healthcare, agriculture, public administration, and economic development. But access must be equitable. The technology shaping humanity's future must not create another divide between those countries that can afford to innovate and those that cannot. and access alone will not be enough. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in our economies and societies, we must develop credible AI governance frameworks that encourage innovation while protecting people, privacy, security, democratic values, and public trust. Technology must remain a tool for human development, not a replacement for human responsibility. We must prepare young people not only to use new technologies, but to question them, govern them, and deploy them ethically. Mr. President, Grenada approaches the future with confidence. We recognize the challenges before us, but we also see enormous possibilities. Our Vision 75 embodies our determination to build a stronger, healthier, a more resilient and more prosperous Grenada. Our commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals reflects our belief in shared global progress, and our engagement in this United Nations reflects our conviction that partnership remains one of humanity's greatest sources of strength. But partnership must deliver. So let this Assembly send a clear message. Let us restore hope in Haiti. Let us protect children and civilians wherever conflict threatens their lives. Let us choose dialogue over division. Let us allow cooperation with Cuba and with all nations to be guided by the interests and well-being of people. Let us ensure that small island developing states have fair access to the financing necessary to build resilience before disaster strikes. Let us equip our young people. to lead the technological transformation rather than become casualties of it. Let us protect our oceans and our planet, and let us transform our multilateral institutions so that they deliver not simply promises, but progress. The measure of this United Nations cannot only be the resolutions we adopt. It must be the lives we improve, the children we protect, the conflict we help prevent, the opportunities we create, and the hope we restore. Mr. President, Grenada stands ready to work with all member states and the international partners in advancing a future that is peaceful, resilient, inclusive, and sustainable. One year ago, Grenada came before this assembly with a message about resilience and education. Today, we build upon that message. Resilience gives us the strength to endure. Transformation gives us the power to change. Partnership gives us the ability to do both. Together, through renewed trust and genuine partnership, We can build a United Nation that delivers, a United Nation that protects, a United Nations that listens, a United Nation that acts, and ultimately, a world in which no country, no community, and no person is left behind. May God bless the United Nations. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the Chair of the delegation of Grenada. I now give the floor to Her Excellency Cecilia Adut Majok Adeng, Chair of the delegation of South Sudan.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I bring you warm greetings and best wishes from His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit, the President of the Republic of South Sudan. And I bring you greetings from the government and the people of South Sudan, together with a message of peace, unity, development, and unwavering commitment to international cooperation. I wish to congratulate Mr. President on your election to preside over the 81st session of this General Assembly. I also express South Sudan's appreciation to the Secretary-General. His Excellency Antonio Guterres has continued his service until the last speech he delivered here early last week. His commitment to the principle of the United Nations Charter stands with us. Mr. President, the theme of this session, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a United Nation that delivers for all, speaks directly to the experience and the aspiration of the people of South Sudan. As the world's youngest nation and the 193rd member of the United Nations, South Sudan understands both the promises and the possibilities of multilateralism. South Sudan also understand that trust is fundamental to peace. trust among citizens, trust between citizens and their institutions, trust among nations, and trust between member states and the international institutions created to serve them. South Sudan remains committed to the United Nations and the purpose and the principle of its charter. We recognize and appreciate the contribution the United Nations has made to South Sudan, from humanitarian assistance and protection of civilians to peacebuilding, development, and institutional support. However, restoring trust also requires honest reflection. Our experience has shown that international institutions can sometimes be slow to adjust to changing circumstances on the ground. Approaches designed to respond to conflict must be capable of evolving as nations move towards peace, recovery, institution building, and ownership. For South Sudan, therefore, restoring trust must mean strengthening partnership between the United Nations and member states, respecting national ownership, recognizing progress while acknowledging remaining challenges, and ensuring that international engagements ultimately strengthen the capacity of the nations to assume the responsibility of their own future. Mr. President, to understand where South Sudan seeks to go, one must understand where South Sudan has came from. The history of South Sudan did not begin with the independence of the 9th of July, 2011. It was shaped by more than half of a century of struggle, sacrifices, displacement, and unwavering desire for freedom and self-determination. Our late Dr. John Garang de Mabior summarized those aspirations of the struggle that when he spoke freedom, liberty, equality, justice, human rights, and democracy. Those aspirations did not end with the independence. They remain part of the ongoing work of nation building. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005 provided the political framework that transformed struggles, decades of struggles, into a peaceful exercise of self-determination. South Sudan, therefore, continues to recognize the indispensable contribution of IGAD and our African Union brothers and sisters. as well as the support of the troika, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Norway, and the wider international community. South Sudan also remembers the extraordinary contribution of the churches and faith-based leaders. During some of the darkest years of the conflict, churches remained with the people of South Sudan. They educated children. They assisted displaced communities, they mediated disputes, and kept alive the belief that reconciliation was possible. That tradition continued with the historical and medical pilgrimage of peace to South Sudan by His Holiness Pope Francis, the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the moderator of the Church of Scotland. Their message reinforced something that South Sudan has learned through painful experience. The message reinforced something that peace requires political agreement. But lasting peace also requires reconciliation, forgiveness, and courage. Mr. President, His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit belongs to the generation that carried the struggle of liberation. Following the passing of Dr. John Garang Dima Bure, President Kiir assumed the responsibility of safeguarding the Comprehensive Peace Agreement. and leading the people of South Sudan towards the referendum on self-determination. On January 2011, the people of South Sudan overwhelmingly spoke through the ballot. And on the 9th of July 2011, President Kiir stood before the people as the flag of the Republic of South Sudan was raised for the first time. 15 years later, South Sudan has traveled a difficult road. There have been achievements. There also have been setbacks. South Sudan experienced internal conflict shortly after independence. Implementation of the revitalized peace agreement has taken longer than originally intended or anticipated. Economic and humanitarian challenges remain significant. The government does not deny these realities, but neither should these challenges be allowed to erase the progress made or define permanently the identity of the Republic of South Sudan. Throughout the transition period, President Kiir has repeatedly made one commitment clear. He will not take South Sudan back to war. This commitment has guided his approach to peace process and remain fundamental to his vision for the next chapter of South Sudan. The mission before President Kiir is therefore different from the mission of the liberation years. The liberation struggle sought to give the people of South Sudan the right to determine their destiny. The responsibility today is to consolidate peace, strengthen institution, and create conditions through which the people of South Sudan can once again determine their political future through democratic means. Mr. President, when the people of South Sudan voted for the independence, they were voting for more than creation of a new state. They were voting for a dream. They dreamt of a peace after generations of war. They dreamt of schools for their children. health care for their families, roads connecting their communities, food security and economic opportunities, justice and equality, strong institutions, and a government whose authority ultimately drives from the will of its people. The difficulties of the last 15 years have been not extinguished, not to extinguish those dreams. They remain alive among the people of South Sudan. And it's precisely for this reason that His Excellency President Salva remains committed to paving the way towards general elections scheduled for December 2026. These elections are intended to mark the conclusion of the transition period and provide the people of South Sudan the opportunity to choose democratically their own leaders. We recognize the important work ahead. Electoral institutions require adequate resources, political dialogue must continue, security arrangements must advance, civic and voter education must reach communities. Women and young people must participate meaningfully. Refugees and internally displaced persons must not be left out. And an environment must be created to which political competition can occur peacefully. The government remains committed to working towards these objectives. For far too long, South Sudan has often been seen internationally through the lens of conflict, humanitarian needs, and political crisis. President Kiir's vision is to create the condition in which the world can once again see the people of South Sudan for who they truly are, a resilient people who struggled for freedom, voted peacefully for independence, continue to aspire for peace, dignity, democracy, and prosperity. The people of South Sudan must increasingly speak for themselves, and they must speak through the ballot. Our journey, therefore, continues from liberation struggle to comprehensive peace agreement to the referendum to independence, from conflict to peace, and now from transition towards democratic governance. Mr. President, the message of President Kiir remains clear-- South Sudan must not return to war. Political disagreement must not be addressed. Political disagreement must be addressed through dialogue. Political competition must never again become armed confrontation. The ballot must replace the bullets. South Sudan recognizes that conducting peaceful elections requires security and strong institutions. The government bears the primary responsibility for protecting its citizens. maintaining public order, and safeguarding the electoral process. South Sudan, therefore, continues to call for constructive engagements with the Security Council concerning restrictive measures, including the arms embargo. South Sudan's objective is not militarization. The objective is to develop professional, unified, disciplined, and accountable security forces operating under the civilian authority and the rule of law. South Sudan believes that accountability and national capacity should reinforce themselves. We therefore call for the lifting of all the restrictive measures, sanctions, and sanctions must be instruments for achieving clear defined objectives. They should not become permanent substitute for political engagements and institution buildings. Mr. President, South Sudan remains grateful for the contribution of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan. We recognize the men and women who serve under the United Nations flag, particularly those who have lost their lives in the service of peace. As South Sudan advances its transition, international engagement must also evolve. President Kiir's vision is not for South Sudan to remain indefinitely dependent upon international peacekeeping. The objective must be a South Sudan capable of sustaining its own peacekeeping. South Sudan, therefore, calls for a greater emphasis on peacebuilding, institutional development, continuous capacity building, and we are also keen to establishing partnership. Invest in South Sudan police and judiciary. Invest in public administration. Invest in education and healthcare. Invest in infrastructure. Invest in women and young people. Invest in institutions that will sustain peace long after peacekeepers have departed. The ultimate measures of a successful peacekeeping should be the establishment of condition under which peacekeeping is no longer required. South Sudan, therefore, seeks a responsible transition from managing crisis towards building a lasting national capacity. Mr. President, peace cannot be sustained without development. At independence, South Sudan inherited extremely limited infrastructure and institutional capacity. Nation building, state building, and service delivery have, therefore, have to proceed simultaneously. President Kiir has placed particular emphasis on agriculture, infrastructure, education, healthcare, and economic diversification. South Sudan possesses millions of hectares of arable land, significant water resources, livestock, fishery, natural resources, and one of the youngest population in the world. South Sudan, therefore, seeks to transition progressively from humanitarian dependency to self reliance, and towards a sustainable development and investment. For a farmer, a road to a market is development. For a child, a functioning school is development. For a mother, access to health care is development. For a young person, employment is development. And for South Sudan, development is one of the strongest foundation for lasting peace. We therefore invite international partners and responsible investors to look beyond South Sudan's current challenges and recognize its potential. Do not ask only what South Sudan needs, ask what South Sudan can offer. Mr. President, South Sudan continues to face severe consequences from climate shocks, despite contributing minimally to global emission. Recurrent floods, droughts, displacement, and food insecurity are affecting millions of South Sudanese. South Sudan, therefore, reiterates its call for predictable and accessible climate financing, investment in adaptation, resilient infrastructure, renewable energy, agriculture, and technology transfer. Climate justice must reflect not only in commitments, but in the implementation. Mr. President, South Sudan and young people, women and young people of South Sudan are essential to President Kiir's vision. The revitalized peace agreement provided 35% representation for women in public institutions. South Sudan continues on working to translate those commitment into meaningful participation at all levels. South Sudan also is an overwhelmingly young population. These young people should not inherit a conflict of previous generation. They should inherit opportunities of peace, education, vocational training, technology, entrepreneurship, agriculture, and sports. That is the future they deserve. Mr. President, decades of conflict scattered South Sudanese across the world. But South Sudanese diaspora should not be viewed only through the history of displacement. It is also an extraordinary national resources. Our national basketball team, the Bright Star, demonstrated this before the world. South Sudanese whose journey had taken them across different countries and continents came together under one flag. Under the leadership of Luol Deng and the South Sudan Basketball Federation, South Sudan qualified for the Basketball World Cup and subsequently the Olympic Games. They showed the world the image of South Sudan, not conflict, not displacement, but talent, discipline, unity, and excellence. This experience offers a model for national development. South Sudan doctors abroad can contribute to health care. Engineers can contribute to infrastructure. Academians can strengthen education. Entrepreneurs can invest and create employment. Technology professionals can conduct, can connect South Sudan to digital economy. And successful South Sudanese around the world can mentor the next generation. To the international community. We need to create a stronger partnership that would enable South Sudan diaspora to transfer their skills and professional experience in order to contribute to the ongoing development in the Republic of South Sudan. To the South Sudanese diaspora, our message is simple. South Sudan needs you. Bring your knowledge home, bring your experience home, bring your investment home, and bring your networks home. Where physical return is not possible, allow your skills and experience to contribute to South Sudan. The same experience, the same spirits that brought South Sudanese athletes from around the world together under one flag can help bring South Sudanese expertise together for one national purpose. South Sudan's greatest resources is ultimately its people, both at home and abroad. Mr. President, South Sudan stand in solidarity with the people of Sudan. South Sudan and Sudan share history, families, economic interests, and one of the longest border in the region. South Sudan, therefore, reiterates its ongoing and continued full support for a lasting peace in the Sudan. South Sudan knows from the experience that military confrontation ultimately requires a political solution. Even the longest conflict must eventually reach a negotiated settlement. South Sudan therefore supports regional and international efforts aimed at achieving peace in Sudan. Outstanding matters arising from the comprehensive peace agreement, including the border issues and the final status of Abyei, also requires a peaceful engagement between South Sudan and Sudan. Mr. President, restoring trust also requires reform of institutions of global governance. The composition of the Security Council does not equitably reflect the realities of today. Africa, with 54 member states, remains without a permanent representation on the Council. South Sudan, therefore, reaffirms its support for the common African position. Africa must be appropriately represented in both permanent and non-permanent categories. Similarly, Developing countries must have a stronger voice in international financial institutions and decisions concerning development, financing, debt, climate, and technology. Reforms do not weaken multilateralism. Reforms strengthen its legitimacy. Mr. President, 15 years after the independence, South Sudan remains a young nation undertaking the difficult work of building a state while consolidating peace and delivering development. The journey has not been easy, but the liberation generation fought for freedom. The generation of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement secured the pathway to self-determination. The people of South Sudan chose independence through the ballots. and His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit carried the responsibility of leading South Sudan through referendum and into statehood. Today, President Kiir's vision is directed towards another historical responsibility, to preserve peace, strengthen national institutions, pave the way towards elections through which the people of South Sudan can determine the next chapter of their nation. This ultimately about completing the promise of independence. A South Sudan at peace with itself, a South Sudan governed through strong institutions, a South Sudan where political competition does not lead to war, a South Sudan where women participate fully and where young people have opportunities. where refugees can return home, where the diaspora can contribute to national development, and where children grow up knowing South Sudan not through the memoirs of war, but through the possibilities of peace. Dr. John Garang once challenged the people of South Sudan to unite and dream together. That dream did not end with independence. It continues today. And today, the responsibility of President Kiir is, and his government, is the political leadership, is indeed, is that people of South Sudan must dream and must have a functioning, peaceful, and a prosperous South Sudan. To our international partners who stood with us during our liberation struggle, and during the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, and during the referendum, and at independence, We say, stand with South Sudan again. But let this chapter be a partnership that strengthen national ownership, a partnership that build institutions, a partnership that recognizes progress while helping address remaining challenges, a partnership that enables South Sudan progressively to stand on its own. Mr. President, for South Sudan, restoring trust means delivering on the promises of peace. Managing transformation means moving from conflict to institutions, from dependency to national capacity, and from transition towards democratic governance. And a United Nations that deliver for all means ultimately help nations develop the capacity to deliver for their own people. South Sudan remains committed to the United Nations. South Sudan remain committed to Africa. And South Sudan remained committed to peace. And under the leadership of His Excellency, President Salva Kiir Mayardit, South Sudan remains committed to the long journey of transforming the sacrifices of liberation into peace, dignity, development, democratic future for which the people of South Sudan have waited for generations. That is the promise of independence. That is the responsibility of this generation, and that is the future South Sudan seek to build. May the Lord Almighty bless the people of South Sudan, and may the Lord Almighty bless all the nation represented in this Assembly. I thank you for your kind attention.
I thank the chair of delegation of South Sudan. I now give the floor to Her Excellency Christina Marcus Lassen, Chair of Delegation of Denmark.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. A compass does not change with the weather. It helps you find a way in fair weather as well as in storm. 81 years ago, the world gave itself a compass. We named it the United Nations Charter. It has helped us stay the course, even when the seas have been anything but calm. It has pointed us toward a world of equal rights, self-determination of peoples, and territorial integrity of all states. large and small, towards a rules-based international order. The progress has been real. More than a billion people lifted out of poverty, standards of living transformed, colonial empires brought to an end, independent nations emerged, peoples gained the right to shape their own future. That progress was made possible because we kept consulting the compass. because we stayed the course. Today, it seems we are losing our way. Wars and conflicts are at the highest level since World War II. Extreme poverty is on the rise. Extreme weather and climate-related disasters are hitting record highs. Mistrust, polarization, and divisions are growing, both among states and within societies. Even the most basic principles of international law, including international humanitarian law, are violated with impunity. To get back on track, we must turn our attention to the compass. Excellencies, respect for the Charter, for human rights, for international law, is not a courtesy we extend when convenient. These are binding obligations we all agree to. Respecting them is the precondition for international peace and security. We see this clearly in Ukraine. Russia's illegal war of choice could end tomorrow if Russia withdrew to its own territory and stopped trying to redraw borders by force. The vast majority of UN member states and the UN Secretary-General support calls for an immediate and comprehensive ceasefire in Ukraine. It is the only basis for good faith talks aimed at a just and lasting peace in line with international law, including the UN Charter. Ukraine has been offering this for a year now. Denmark's support to Ukraine will remain steadfast. This is not only a matter of helping Ukraine defend itself. It is a matter of defending the universal principles upon which this organization was built. Excellencies, in Sudan, the war continues to inflict immense human suffering. Millions are displaced. Famine has been confirmed. And the international community has been warned of mass atrocities over and over again, but has failed to act. The responsibility for this horrific war lies in the hand of the warring parties, yet it is fueled by outside actors and permitted by international inaction. We must act now to prevent further mass atrocities against the Sudanese people. We must put our political will and weight behind a stronger demand for peace and accountability. The warring parties must come to the negotiation table, engage in dialogue, and agree to a much-needed truce. Denmark fully supports the Quint's efforts to advance a civilian-led political process and welcomes the improved coordination among mediators. Excellencies, in Syria, the fall of the brutal Assad regime offers a historic opportunity to build a brighter future for all Syrians. Denmark is committed to supporting the people of Syria in a Syrian-led and owned transition. It is a glimpse of hope in a troubled region, and a stark contrast to the destabilizing actions of Iran, whose consequences are felt far beyond the region. Denmark's position remains clear. Iran must never be allowed to develop or acquire a nuclear weapon. We strongly support continued diplomatic efforts to restore effective international verification of Iran's nuclear program. And we deeply regret the unwillingness of a few Council members to acknowledge that sanctions measures have been reinstated in full accordance with Security Council Resolution 2231. At the same time, We urge Iran to comply fully with Resolution 2817, cease attacks against countries in the region, and refrain from any actions or threats that undermine the freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. Excellencies, last year, this Assembly endorsed the New York Declaration, a roadmap towards the two-state solution, a path to lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians. Since then, The comprehensive plan to end the Gaza conflict has been endorsed by the Security Council. Now it must be implemented in full. We call on all parties to stay committed to the plan. Yet in Gaza, civilians continue to pay the price. Far more must be done to secure humanitarian access and long-term peace. And in the occupied West Bank, settler violence and settlement expansion threaten the daily lives of Palestinians, and undermine the prospects for a future Palestinian state. This has to stop. Excellencies, as an elected member of the Security Council, Denmark strives to ensure that the Council fulfills its mandate. At times, we succeed. This June, the Security Council unanimously adopted resolution 2823 on accountability for crimes against UN peacekeepers led by Denmark and Pakistan, and backed by a record 153 Member States. A clear signal of commitment to the safety and security of the brave men and women who serve under the UN flag. And a clear demonstration that the Council can still come together and speak with one voice. Too often, however, the Security Council is blocked by geopolitical divisions, unable to act. Meanwhile, the costs of inaction are felt by the civilians across the world as the disrespect for international humanitarian law is allowed to fester. Excellencies, our collective inability to halt the killings, suffering, and injustices in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, and beyond must not prompt us to surrender to a world ruled by brute force. On the contrary, it must inspire us to work harder to sustain and strengthen the structures, instruments and mechanisms we have built over the last 81 years. To Denmark, this includes maintaining our firm support for the ICJ and the ICC as core international justice institutions. This year, Denmark nominated its first ever candidate for judge at the ICC, reaffirming our unwavering support for the Court at a critical time. It also means continuing to meet the UN target of providing 0.7% of GNI for official development assistance. For more than 45 years, Denmark has consistently delivered on that goal. We do so not as an act of altruism, but because it's in our shared interest. It creates jobs, opportunities, and hope where people live, allowing them to build a future at home increasing stability and mutual prosperity. We call on fellow member states to join us. At the current juncture, however, sustaining an order with the UN as its core means working for reform. Reform is how we keep this organization fit for the world we live in. Denmark continues to call for a fundamental Security Council reform. We wish to expand the Council with more members in both categories, including permanent seat, for underrepresented regions. And we wish to commence text-based negotiations. Only then can we begin to redress historical injustices. Denmark also strongly supports the UN80 reform process. We applaud the results so far and call for ambitions to be raised. We must strive to build a more efficient and inclusive UN, a UN that delivers better on its core mandates and underground where it matters most. To enable this, we call on all UN member states to meet their financial obligations to the UN in full and on time. Excellencies, let's be real. We need the UN, not for the sake of the UN, but in order to address challenges that face us all. Because no single country can manage climate change, global health threats, or the governance of emerging technologies on its own. The climate crisis makes the point starkly. We see it in droughts and wildfires, in record-breaking heat, and in the growing pressure on food, water, and energy accessibility and security. The challenge before us is no longer a lack of solutions. We have the solutions. We know what's required. Now we need to deliver. Therefore, COP31 must be a COP of implementation, turning ambition into action and real-world results, delivering on the objectives of the Paris Agreement and its 1.5 degrees Celsius temperature goal. With only four years left to 2030, we must also be honest about where we stand on sustainable development goals, both in terms of achievements and challenges. Let's make the upcoming SDG Summit a turning point, 2030 must not be a missed deadline. Excellencies, this year we will be selecting a new Secretary-General. Denmark thanks Secretary-General Guterres for a decade of dedicated service to this Organization, often under exceptionally difficult circumstances. The next Secretary-General will take over an Organization under strain and under scrutiny. To bring the UN safely into the future, we must select a person who can work to restore global trust in the UN and among its Member States. Excellencies, in closing, I am happy to inform you that last week, in this very building, Denmark, Greenland and the United States signed an agreement on security which strengthens the defence of Greenland, the NATO area and the American continent. The agreement is good for Greenland, for Denmark, for the United States, for NATO and Europe, and for international peace and security. Progress can still be made when we consult the COMPASS. I thank you.
I thank the chair of delegation of Denmark. I now give the floor to his Excellency Boris Vazir, Mark, Johnny Carrero, chair of delegation of Costa Rica.

Mr. President. With a great sense of humility and respect, I address you and the excellencies here in this illustrious hall. More than eight decades ago, the founders of the United Nations understood that no peace built on brute force could stand the test of time. They opted instead for law, cooperation, and dialogue as pillars of a new international order. Today, this conviction is facing one of the toughest tests it has faced since the organization's foundation. The world stands at a period of deep-rooted fragmentation. The world is deeply polarized. Armed conflicts are dragging on longer than before. Transnational organized crime is broadening its capacity to act. Its tentacles are growing longer. The effects of climate change are growing ever more intense. Development divides remain, and the technological transformation is posing unprecedented challenges to our institutions. At the same time, trust in multilateralism is waning precisely when we need it most. Standing before this landscape, Costa Rica reaffirms its belief that no state, no state can alone address challenges that are common to us all. Multilateralism is a prerequisite for the preservation of peace, to promote sustainable development and to protect human dignity. However, multilateralism will only preserve its dignity if it proves able to yield tangible results, specific results for people, for human beings. Costa Rica champions a United Nations which is more agile, more efficient, more transparent, and more accountable to its member states. organization should establish priorities, do away with overlaps, make prudent use of its resources and measure its results. President, international peace and security are facing increasingly complex threats. Mr. President of the General Assembly, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. President, I have the honor to address this Assembly on behalf of the government and the people of the Republic of Vanuatu. I bring with me the voice of a nation of more than 80 islands, of many indigenous communities and languages, and a nation whose identity has been shaped by the ocean, by custom, by faith, by resilience, and above all, by commitment to peace. Mr. Secretary-General, this session also carries a particular significance for us because it is the final high-level General Assembly of your tenure as Secretary-General of the United Nations. On behalf of the government and people of Vanuatu, I wish to convey a profound appreciation for your service to the United Nations and your engagement with the people of the Pacific. Your visits to our region reflect an understanding that the concerns of small island development states deserve to be heard at a higher level. Over the course of your tenure, You have led United Nations through some of the most tumultuous periods in recent international history. You have stood consistently for multilateralism at a time when multilateralism itself was under enormous pressure. Vanuatu hopes that the next Secretary-General will carry forward that same commitment to all member states, large or small. Mr. President, Fernando comes to this 81st session of the General Assembly with a simple message: the world needs the United Nations more than ever, and the United Nations must deliver for the people who depend on it. The theme of this session, "Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all," therefore comes at an important moment. The 81st session opened against a backdrop of profound geopolitical uncertainty and rapid transformation. For Vanuatu, developments in international system are never distant or abstract. The effects reach our villages, our markets, our schools, our hospitals, our oceans, and our homes. Mr. President, the international political and security environment is becoming increasingly difficult. We are witnessing geopolitical competition, strategic rivalry, armed conflicts, growing military expenditures, economic fragmentation, technological disruption, and a weakening of confidence in the multilateral institutions. The rules that were designed to provide predictability and stability are increasingly being tested. The prohibition against the use of force is being challenged. The international humanitarian law is being tested. The peaceful settlements of dispute is being undermined, and the authority of international institution is being questioned. For small states, this is deeply concerning. Small states do not possess the military, economic, or technological capabilities of major powers. We do not have the ability to impose our will through cohesion. Our security depends fundamentally on something else, international law, multilateral institutions, diplomacy, and the equal sovereignty of states. This is why Vanuatu has a profound interest in the success of the United Nations. The Charter begins with a commitment to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war and reaffirms the equal rights of nations, large and small. It establishes sovereign equality, peaceful settlement of disputes, and the prohibition or the threat or use of force as fundamental principles of international relations. These are not merely legal concepts for Vanuatu. They are our security architecture. When international law is respected, a small nation has protection. When the Charter is respected, a small state has a voice. When disputes are resolved peacefully, a small state does not have to choose between submission and confrontation. And when sovereignty is respected, independence has meaning. We therefore cannot accept a world in which international law applies differently according to the size, military strength, or economic power of a state. The Charter must apply equally to all. Mr. President, the security environment is also changing in ways that are particularly important for the Pacific region. The Pacific Islands are increasingly viewed through the lens of strategic competition. There is growing interest in our maritime spaces, our sea lanes, our resources, and our geopolitical location. We welcome genuine partnerships, but we also say clearly, the Pacific must not become an arena for great power competition at the expense of Pacific priorities. The security of the Pacific is not simply about military deployments or strategic competition. For us, security also means food security, energy security, water security, health security, economic security, cybersecurity, environmental security, and the security of our people from the impacts of climate change. For Vanuatu, a cyclone that destroys a school is a security issue. A rise in food and energy prices, as recently experienced by Middle East conflict is a security issue. A disrupted shipping route is a security issue. A cyber attack against critical infrastructure is a security issue. Sea level rise also raises fundamental questions on sovereignty, identity, and security. Vanuatu joins its Pacific colleagues in affirming the continuity of statehood and the preservation of maritime zone and sovereign rights in the face of sea level rise. The rights and dignity of affected persons must remain at the center of international response. These are realities faced by small island developing states. We therefore call for a broader understanding of international peace and security, one that reflects the realities of small island developing states. And we hope that these security concerns are well understood here at the United Nations. Mr. President, What happens here in New York does not remain here in New York. The decisions taken by major powers affect the smallest economies. A conflict thousands of kilometers away can increase the price of oil in Vanuatu. A disruption in international shipping can increase the price of food in our islands. A change in global interest rates can increase the cost of borrowing. A crisis in international development finance can delay a school, a hospital, a road or a climate resilience project. And global economic uncertainty can affect tourism, investment, employment and government revenue. For Vanuatu, therefore, foreign policy and domestic development are inseparable. Our international diplomacy is ultimately about our people. It is about whether a child in Tanna can attend school, whether a farmer in Malekula can bring a produce to market, whether a family in Toba has access to reliable electricity, whether a community in Penama can recover quickly after a natural disaster. and whether our young people can find meaningful opportunities at home rather than being forced to leave in search of them. Mr. President, this year, as Vanuatu celebrated its 46th independence anniversary, we reflected on how far our country has come since 1980. Our independence was not given to us in a golden place. It was achieved through the determination, courage and sacrifice of our people, supported by our brothers and sisters in the Pacific. At our independence celebrations, we were reminded once again of the importance of solidarity, including the historic support of Papua New Guinea during our struggle for independence. Our 46th Independence anniversary was therefore not simply a celebration of the past. It was a call to build the future. The message of a national celebration was one of unity, national pride, resilience, and determination to build a stronger, more prosperous Vanuatu for future generations. And this is important in the context of our discussions today. Vanuatu has experienced cyclones, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and economic shocks and other disasters. Yet we continue to stand. We rebuild, we adapt, and we move forward. Resilience is not simply something Vanuatu speaks about. It is something our people practice every day. But resilience also requires international solidarity. A small island country cannot finance all of its resilient needs alone. We cannot rebuild every road, bridge, school, and hospital after every disaster from domestic resources alone. We cannot absorb indefinitely the economic consequences of external shocks, and we cannot protect our people from a changing climate without a meaningful international cooperation. Therefore, when we speak about climate finance, development finance, disaster resilience, and sustainable development, we are not asking merely for charity. We are asking for partnership, fairness, and the fulfillment of international commitments. That partnership must include predictable and accessible finance for adaptation and for addressing loss and damage. Access to such finance must be made easier for the small island developing island state and must respond to the needs of our communities. We invite partners to support our Pacific Resilience Facility in bringing the necessary resources to support resilience efforts in the Pacific. At the same time, keeping 1.5 degrees Celsius is vital for the Pacific. In light of the International Court's advisory opinion, we urge all members to give effect to their legal obligations through stronger climate actions and international cooperation. Mr. President, we are also deeply concerned by the developing strong El Nino event in the Pacific, which threatens to bring more extreme heat, disrupted rainfall, drought, and flooding across the region. For Pacific Island countries, these are not simply meteorological events. They affect food and water security, agriculture, fisheries, health, livelihoods, and the resilience of already vulnerable communities. The international community must act before disaster strikes. We call for stronger regional early warning system, pre-positioned humanitarian assistance, rapid access to climate and disaster financing, and greater investment in resilient infrastructure and food and water security. The Pacific does not ask the world to prevent El Nino. We ask the world to help us to prepare for it, withstand its impacts, and recover with dignity. Mr. President, the ocean is central to Vanuatu's identity, culture, food security, and prosperity. Protection of it is essential for the future of our people. Climate change, damage to the ocean and loss of biodiversity are linked. We must address them together. Vanuatu welcomes the entry into force of the BBNJ Agreement. It is an important achievement for ocean governance and multilateral cooperation. For a nation whose identity, culture, and prosperity are inseparable from the ocean, the BBNJ Agreement represents an important step towards protecting marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction and ensuring that the benefits of a common ocean heritage are shared fairly and sustainably. Vanuatu stands ready to contribute to its effective implementation and to strengthening international cooperation for the protection of our oceans for generations to come. Since the agreement entered into force on 17 January 2026, following its ratification by more than 60 states, including Vanuatu and our Pacific neighbors, the international community has moved into a critical implementation phase. One ought to look forward to the first conference of the parties advancing the operationalization of marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits from marine genetic resources. And we call on all states yet to ratify the agreement to do so without delay. The implementation of the BBNJ Agreement must respect sovereign rights and take full account of the special circumstances and capacity constraints of small island developing states. It must enable countries to participate effectively and equally benefit from it. The hosting of the inaugural Melanesian Ocean Summit in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea, this year arrives at a critical juncture where, on one hand, we are faced with daily mounting challenges of the detrimental effects of climate change, the alarming degradation of our marine biodiversity, pervasive marine pollution, and the over-exploitation of our vital marine resources. Yet, some of these global issues have already escalated to a level where ensuring sustainability for future generations has become a critical concern, highlighting the urgent need for improved management of our ocean resources. In today's world, science and technology and economic opportunities must also work closely with our traditional custodians in our vast coastal area to maintain respect for nature. Our culture and tradition are deeply rooted in the ocean, and hence our collective wisdom and collaboration to address the core issues affecting our people's livelihoods today and reshape the future of our ocean and communities is extremely paramount. Mr. President, the world is entering a period of extraordinary transformation. Artificial intelligence is changing economies and societies. Digital technologies are changing the way governments operate. Energy systems are changing. Global trade is changing. Demographic patterns are changing. And climate change is transforming the physical environment in which many of our societies exist. The question before us is, us is not whether transformation will occur. It will. The question is, who will shape the transformation and who will benefit from it? For Vanuatu, the answer must be clear. Transformation must not create a new hierarchy between those who possess technology, capital and influence, and those who merely experience the consequences. We need an international system in which developing countries and small states are participants in transformation, not simply consumers of made elsewhere. Artificial intelligence provides one example. AI offers enormous opportunities for education, healthcare, public administration, agriculture, climate forecasting and economic development. But without appropriate governance, it could also deepen existing inequalities. Small states need access to technology. We need digital infrastructure. We need skills and capacity. We need access to data and computing. And we need a meaningful voice in establishing the international norms that govern emerging technologies. The digital future must not become another form of dependency. Mr. President. There is a tendency to describe small states primarily in terms of our vulnerabilities. We are small, we are geographically dispersed, we are economically vulnerable, we have limited institutional capacity, we depend on international markets, we depend on development partners, we depend on international shipping, we depend on imported fuel, food, and manufactured goods. And yes, in many respects, we are dependent on the international system, but dependence must not be confused with powerlessness. Small states can lead. Indeed, history has shown that some of the most important developments in international law and global governance have emerged because small and vulnerable states refuse to remain silent. Vanuatu is proud of its commitment to the global climate debate. We are proud of our advocacy for climate justice. We are proud of our role in advancing the recognition of the legal dimensions of climate change, and we remain committed to ensuring that the voices of those most vulnerable to climate change are heard in international decision-making. In this vein, the Vanuatu government wholeheartedly thank all the UN members who have supported us in this journey, especially here at the UN General Assembly and the International Court of Justice. Our experience demonstrates an important principle, influence is not determined solely by population, territory, or military power. Influence can come from ideas. It can come from moral authority. It can come from coalition building. It can come from persistence. It can come from international law. And it can come from the ability to bring different regions and groups together around a common cause. This is the strength of the General Assembly. Every Member State has a voice. Every Member State has a vote. And every Member State, large or small, has a responsibility to contribute. The General Assembly is the most representative body of the United Nations, bringing together all 193 members on the basis of sovereign equality. For countries such as Vanuatu, this principle is fundamental. Mr. President. The imposition of coercive economic measures, including unilateral sanctions against developing countries, is unfair and unjust. Such measures are in violation with the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and adversely affect sustainable development outcomes of countries such as Cuba. In this respect, we consistently call for the uplift of the economic embargo on the Republic of Cuba. Mr. President, peace and security cannot be separated from human rights. Vanuatu remains deeply concerned about reports of serious human rights violations affecting indigenous Papuans in West Papua. United Nations special procedures have also raised concerns regarding indigenous rights, displacement, cultural rights, environmental impacts, and the treatment of human rights defenders in Papua. The call from the Pacific Forum leaders for the UN human rights commissioner visit to West Papua remains unheeded and needs to be actioned. Mr. President, Vanuatu reaffirms its unwavering support for the decolonization of Kanaky, New Caledonia, which remains a non-self-governing territory under the purview of the United Nations. We reiterate the inalienable right of the Indigenous Kanak people to self-determination and call for a peaceful, inclusive, transparent, and credible process consistent with the Charter of the United Nations and relevant General Assembly resolutions. We remain concerned by the persistent social economic disparities affecting the Kanak people, including inequalities in employment, education, income, and access to economic opportunities. These long-standing structural imbalances continue to constrain the full and equitable enjoyment of economic, social, and cultural rights by Indigenous Kanaks, notwithstanding the territory's considerable natural resources and economic potential. Reports from the case supported by independent assessment point to the enduring effects of economic marginalization and uneven development, which may be understood as forms of structural violence insofar as they limit meaningful participation in and inequitable benefit from the territory's development. Addressing these disparities is essential to fostering social cohesion and advancing a just, inclusive, and sustainable decolonization process. In this regard, Vanuatu calls for the full implementation of relevant United Nations resolutions on the question of New Caledonia and encourages continued engagement and constructive dialogue among all stakeholders, including the administering power and the representatives of the Kanak people. We further reaffirm the important role of the Special Committee on Decolonization and the Fourth Committee in advancing the realization of self-determination and ensuring that the rights, aspirations, and interests of the Kanak people remain at the center of decolonization process. Mr. President, at the end of August, the Vanuatu government initiated proceedings against France before the International Court of Justice concerning sovereignty over Umanek and Umanek Leke Islands, or Matthew and Hunter, as they call in English, and the maritime boundaries between Vanuatu and New Caledonia. These islands are an integral part of Vanuatu's territory, grounded in customary governance, longstanding historical connections, indigenous ownership, and is seen as part of our duty as ancestral custodians to protect and preserve. We recognize France as a steadfast champion of the international rules-based order, and under the leadership of President Macron, a strong supporter of international judicial institutions, France has stood alongside Vanuatu in advancing global climate action including through its support for initiatives before the International Court of Justice. We greatly value this partnership and France's leadership on issues of international importance. It is in the same spirit of mutual respect and commitment to international law that we respectfully invite France to consent to the jurisdiction of the Court. Mr. President. Trust is important for the United Nations' credibility. It cannot be restored through declarations alone. Trust must be earned through action. People will trust the United Nations when they see it preventing conflict. They will trust it when international law is respected. They will trust it when humanitarian assistance reaches those who need it. They will trust it when development commitments become real projects. They will trust it when climate finance reaches vulnerable communities. They will trust it when small ahead, and they will trust it when the international system treats all nations with equal dignity. For Vanuatu, restoring trust also means restoring confidence in the multilateral in multilateralism itself. We must resist the temptation to conclude that because the international system is imperfect, it is therefore irrelevant. The UN80 reforms currently implemented are paramount to rebuild trust again at the United Nations and therefore needs to be managed diligently. FANU supports efforts to strengthen the United Nations, but reform must preserve what is most important, the principle of sovereign equality. The United Nations cannot become an institution where the forces of the most powerful states dominate, where smaller states are expected merely to follow. Reform must strengthen General Assembly. It must make international institutions more accessible to developing countries. It must address the financing and capacity constraints facing small delegations. It must strengthen preventive diplomacy. It must improve the implementation of international decisions. It must ensure that the development pillar remains resourced and that the implementation on the ground is effective and efficient. And it must ensure that international law remains central to the international system. Finally, calls for a UN Security Council that is more representative, transparent, and accountable, with membership and working methods that reflect today's realities and give all regions a meaningful voice. But reform cannot be limited to institutional structures. The deeper reform we require is political, a renewed commitment by member states to the principles we have already agreed to. The Charter does not need to be reinvented, it needs to be respected. Mr. President, Excellencies, for Vanuatu, the United Nations Charter remains our compass. It tells us that the nations are sovereign equals. It tells us that disputes must be settled peacefully. It tells us that the force must not be used against the territory or political independence of states. It tells us that the nations must cooperate. It tells us, and it reminds us, that the ultimate purpose of the international system is not power for its own sake. It is peace, justice, human dignity, development and cooperation, and it is better future for succeeding generations. These principles are particularly important to Vanuatu because we know what independence means. Our independence is not merely the absence of colonial rule. Independence means the right of our people to determine our future. It means sovereignty. It means dignity. It means and it means having an equal place in the family of nations. That is why Vanuatu will continue to defend the multilateral system. That is why we will continue to defend international law. And that is why we will continue to speak for the principle that every nation, regardless of size, matters. Mr. President, we meet at a critical moment in international affairs. There are wars that remain unresolved. There are communities facing humanitarian catastrophe. There is growing geopolitical rivalry. There is economic uncertainty. There is climate disruption. There is technological transformation. And there is declining confidence in the international systems. institutions. Yet, I remain convinced that this is precisely the moment when we must choose cooperation over confrontation. We must choose dialogue over division. We must choose law over force. We must choose solidarity over indifference. And we must choose multilateralism over fragmentation. Vanuatu comes from a part of the world where our ancestors navigated vast oceans using the stars, the winds, the currents, and the knowledge passed from generation to generation. Today, the international community is navigating another uncertain ocean. We need a compass. The United Nations Charter is that compass. It provides the principles by which we can navigate a world of competing interests while preserving our common humanity. The theme of this A/15 session, "Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all," reminds us of what is required. But ultimately, restoring trust will depend not on the words we adopt here, but on the actions we take when we leave this hall. Let us, therefore, build a United Nations that is strong enough to prevent war, fair enough to protect the vulnerable, courageous enough to defend international law, and inclusive enough to give every nation a meaningful voice. Let us build a United Nations where the concerns of a small island nation in the Pacific and all over the world can stand alongside those of the largest powers of the world. Let us not allow division to rule our era. Instead, we choose cooperation. We choose peace. We choose justice. We choose solidarity. And we choose to renew our faith in the idea that together, nations can build a world We can build a better world. Vanuatu stands ready to do its part. Thank you.
I thank the Chair of the delegation of Vanuatu. I would now give the floor to His Excellency Marc-Herman Nianadou Araba, Chair of the delegation of Benin.

President of the General Assembly, Secretary-General of the United Nations, Excellencies, Heads of Delegation, ladies and gentlemen, It is a great honor for me to be speaking before this august Assembly. I would like to convey to you the warmest greetings of the Beninese people and to carry before you the voice of these people, a voice resolutely committed to peace, dialogue and multilateralism, a voice which yearns to fully partake in our collective reflection about the future of our organization and the future of our world. If I may, at the outset, I would like to pay a glowing tribute to His Excellency Antonio Guterres. This is his last General Assembly as Secretary-General of the United Nations. At a time when the temptation to withdraw to turn inwards is strong, when many are saying that in the face of crises, We must do so. No nation can build lasting security and prosperity through isolation. I would like to extend to Mr. Guterres our heartfelt gratitude. Thank you for your commitment to serving humanity. I also wish to extend our heartfelt congratulations to His Excellency Khalilur Rahman, President of this 81st session. We wish you every success as you discharge your duties. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, there are moments in history where we are compelled to choose not just what we want to do, but also what we want to become. It is with this reflection in mind that Benin is taking part in this session, driven by a deep-seated conviction. You can't just wait for the future. You have to prepare for it. Now, this conviction serves as a guide for Benin. It's also inspired been in Vision 2060, which is propelling our nation towards the centenary of our independence. But this ambition does not apply only to the fate of our nation. It will also determine the way in which we view the world, the world which today stands at a crossroads. We are seeing wars dragging on, terrorist threats making inroads, persistent geopolitical tensions. worsening inequality, debt levels which are reducing the room for maneuver available to many states, as well as climate upheaval, which is hitting the most vulnerable the hardest. At the same time, we're witnessing technological transformation on a vast scale. It's accelerating. AI is already transforming knowledge, work, our economies, education and information. Never has humanity had so many different means to shape its fate. However, nor has humanity ever been so acutely aware of the need to make collective decisions about how these means should be used to serve the common good. This is why the theme of this 81st session, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a UN that delivers for all, resonates so strongly. The true challenge of our time is not just managing a succession of crises, but it is restoring our collective capacity to anticipate, to make decisions, to act. before these crises become irreversible. Mr. President, Benin believes in multilateralism. We believe not because we harbor nostalgia for the world of 1945, but because in 2026, the world more than ever needs a forum where states can talk to one another, listen to one another, and act in concert. Defending multilateralism also means taking a lucid look at the United Nations Organization. Trust, indeed, is not something you can order. It takes shape when our organization can respond to the expectations of our people, the people it serves, when the organization can deliver concrete results. It is in this spirit that Benin supports the efforts undertaken within the framework of the UN80 initiative. We need to achieve greater efficiency, coherence, transparency and responsibility. Nonetheless, we should remain cognizant of a key requirement. Reforming the UN doesn't simply mean cutting costs. What it should mean is boosting the organization's impact. A more effective United Nations should be better positioned to prevent conflicts, to respond to humanitarian crises, to shore up development, and anticipate the transformations which are already shaping our future. It should also remain true to the principles which underpin its legitimacy, universality, the sovereign equality of states, solidarity, and respect for the UN Charter. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, there is one reform without which all the others will remain incomplete. the reform of the stewardship of international peace and security. The Security Council, for the most part, reflects a balance of forces, the balance of forces in a world which is no longer today's world. Africa does not have a permanent seat. This situation raises issues of justice, equity, and the legitimacy. It calls into question the very legitimacy of the entire multilateral system. Benin would like to reaffirm its unswerving support for the common African position set forth in the Izolwini Consensus and the Siet Declaration. We're not demanding a privilege. We're demanding for the stewardship of international peace and security, for that stewardship to be in keeping with the world we claim to serve. Mr. President, for Benin, the issue of security has a very concrete, a very tangible dimension. Terrorism has hit our subregion. It seeks to exploit our vulnerability, to take advantage of our borders and to progressively extend its clutches to new areas. Benin understands full well just how grave this threat is. On this note, I'd like to solemnly commend the bravery and commitment of our defense and security forces, as well as the resilience of the people of Benin. Our response is resolute. We are strengthening our defense and security capabilities. We are bolstering the surveillance of our territory and our borders. We are also stepping up our cooperation with our neighbors and our partners. However, our region's experience has taught us one very important lesson. When faced with the fast-evolving threat, we must act very quickly. before that threat becomes a crisis. For that reason, prevention, early warning and upstream action should all be part and parcel of our security policy. This requires better intelligence sharing, strengthening cross-border cooperation, improving coordination between national, sub-regional and continent-wide mechanisms. interstate solidarity, regional cooperation, the action of the African Union, the support of the United Nations. We need all of the above to be better coordinated. Education, employment, infrastructure, and the opportunities offered up to our young people are also part and parcel of our efforts aimed at preventing the vulnerabilities very vulnerabilities which terrorist groups seek to exploit. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, collective security can only last if we also have economic and financial security. There is indeed another source of fragility at the international level, and that is the fragility of development financing. Many developing countries are facing a particularly difficult equation. They must accelerate their development and at the same time fund their energy transition as well as adapt to climate change, on top of investing in health, education, the digital sphere, and meeting growing social needs. However, these requirements are piling up against the backdrop of a context where access to funding is increasingly costly, where fiscal space is shrinking. Such a situation is no more sustainable than it is equitable. Therefore, Benin calls for ongoing transformation of the international financial architecture, the objective being to allow developing countries to access more accessible, predictable financing, financing that is better tailored to their development trajectories. We must also have the ambition of investing more in development because investing in development is tantamount to investing in peace, security, and stability. Mr. President, The climate issue is an excellent illustration of this demand for justice. Africa contributes relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions, and yet we are already bearing the full brunt of climate change. We're not asking for the right to pollute. We're asking for the right to development. We would like for adaptation. building resilience and the issue of loss and damage for all of these to be addressed urgently, given the urgency of the reality our people are already facing. We also want for the energy transition to be an opportunity to industrialize, to create jobs and bolster access to energy. The way we see it, climate justice is not about pitting development and transition against one another. I thank the Chair of delegation of Benin. We have heard the last speaker in the general debate. I will now deliver my closing remarks. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, six days

I asked whether we were prepared to confront some hard truths about this organization. I call for honesty, realism, and pragmatism to guide our discussions. Speakers pointed out that effects of conflicts do not stay where they happen. Their impacts reverberate throughout the world.
