We heard that only a few of the sustainable development goals are on track. We heard that progress has stalled. And we heard the question that should trouble us all. Should we have done much more? The answer must be a resounding yes. The burden is not shared equally. Those speaking most urgently about development were often the countries facing the heaviest debt burdens, the narrowest fiscal space, the greatest climate vulnerability, and the least voice in the institutions that shape the global economy. Debt was spoken of more forcefully by those who bear it, not by those with the greatest ability to resolve it. We have heard that we must honor the CVA commitment reform the international financial architecture, provide affordable and accessible finance, expand fiscal space, strengthen productive capacities, and invest in people. And we must deliver on the promise of Paris. Climate disasters are erasing hard-earned development gains and deepening inequality. For small island developing states, low-lying coastal countries, least developed countries, and climate-vulnerable nations, adaptation and resilience are not optional expenditures. World leaders have pointed out that these are matters of survival. Excellencies, human rights, the third pillar of the organization, was another clear thread throughout the general debate. The test of our commitment to human rights is not when they're easy to defend. it is when defending them is difficult. We see the test wherever civilians are dehumanized, wherever minorities face hatred, wherever migrants and refugees are denied dignity, and wherever women and girls are excluded from education, employment, and public life. It was clear from the debate that gender equality cannot remain peripheral to our agenda. They go to the heart of the principles we have gathered here to uphold and defend. Excellencies, the human rights agenda is also moving rapidly into the digital space. Rights must be protected online as they are offline. Member states were clear. Incendiary rhetoric and hate speech, the first step towards dehumanization and violence, are spreading rapidly and taking root across global societies. with hostile actors using automated tools to falsify narratives. We must balance robust protection for vulnerable communities while safeguarding accountability and legitimate expression. Coordinated interventions by governments, companies, civil societies, indeed all of us, are needed to push back against hate. Excellencies, While peace and security, human rights and sustainable development are perennial concerns in this hall, artificial intelligence, including artificial general intelligence, has moved from the margins of our discussions to the center. Four years ago, AI was raised in this hall by only five delegations. This year, 128 delegations addressed it. And this number was more than those who spoke on climate change and human rights. Leader after leader recognized the extraordinary potential of AI to transform public services, accelerate scientific discovery, advance sustainable development, and expand access to knowledge while pointing out potential risks arriving from it. Many framed AI as a question of governance. Who designs it? Who benefits? Who bears the risk? And who is accountable when harm occurs? A delegation emphasized a principle that should guide us all. No machine possesses democratic legitimacy. No algorithm inherits constitutional responsibility. That is the right starting point. AI governance must be human-centered, inclusive, and attentive to the needs of developing countries. It must prevent a new divide in which a smaller number of countries and companies control the data, computing power, and rules that shape everyone's future. Member states must remain at the heart of this work, but they cannot act alone. We must engage industries, scientists, researchers, civil society, academia, young people, the companies building this system, and the people using them. Let us carry that ambition into the global dialogue on AI governance in 2027. Excellencies, the world leaders also spoke clearly about reforming the United Nations. Reform is not an exercise in rearranging structures or reducing budgets or rearranging budget lines. Its measure is whether this organization delivers better, faster, and more fairly for the people it serves. We will build on the UN 80 initiative and the mandate implementation review. No reform agenda, including UN80, is complete without addressing this longstanding inequity in the Security Council. Excellencies, The appointment of the next Secretary-General also emerged as one of this Assembly's most consequential responsibilities at a time when the Organization is facing complex issues and challenges. The Charter is clear about the selection process, that the Security Council will recommend and the General Assembly will appoint the next Secretary-General. Member States called for a process that is transparent inclusive and merit-based. The selection process must strengthen, not diminish, the legitimacy, independence, and moral authority of the office. Excellencies, I chose restoring trust as the principal focus of my presidency. It resonated widely with the speakers during this high-level week and the general debate. We heard of a crisis of institutional trust We were reminded that trust cannot be taken for granted, and we heard a vigorous defense of multilateralism, but not as an end in itself. A delegation observed that the test of multilateralism is not how many resolutions we adopt or how many meetings we hold. Its test is whether collective action changes realities on the ground. All this goes to the heart of the theme of our 81st session, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a United Nations that Delivers for All. Trust cannot be commanded, it must be earned through consistency between words and deeds, equal application of international law, fulfillment of commitments, genuine representation, transparency, accountability, and results. Restoring trust, therefore, means making our institutions worthy of that trust. Meaningful and often painful reforms need to underpin efforts to rebuild trust. These hall, where grievances are aired, differences negotiated, and agreements forged, is one of the humanity's greatest achievements. Let us pursue reform that is meaningful, representative, and fair. and let us restore trust by rebuilding our organization that delivers for all. I thank you. I now come to right of reply.
